div.head: Examiner, Friday, February 13, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Friday, February 13, 1903.

school there. She was such a dreadful little pickle Ala nobody could manage her except Madame Delhane. so mother gave her up as hopeless. I staven't seen the child for nearly two years. I wonder what she's like now; children alter so at her age. Why, she must he seventeen by this time.* "Indeed," said Sir Jasper.

"Shall I write and say we are coming?" • "Yes, by all means if you wish to. We have no one coming until after the 19th, have we? We can go down to Shallowdene on Saturday if you are ready." And Sir Jasper rose to open the door as his wife left the room.

It was very, very sad indeed, the saddest thin?, in fact, that had ever happened in all the seventeen years of Joyce's happy life. In one short week the term would come to an end, and her school- days would be over. She did not like to think of it at all, nor did madame either. The tears would well up into madame's dear old eyes, leaving them red and dim, when she spoke about it to monsieur. But with the complete and blessed optimism of youth, Joyce would thrust the unpleasant thought away from her.

"'Never mind, madame darling," she would say, flinging her impulsive arms round madame's neck with a hug. "I shall come over and live for months and months with you, and you will come and spend all the holidays with us at Shallowdene, and it will be almost exactly like being at school all the time, only heaps and heaps nicer, because there won't be any bothering lessons. And, oh ! isn't it just a lovely, lovely, beautiful world to live in, full of nice people and pretty clothes and things—isn't it ?" She was the happiest little being in creation ; she was always so gay and so wholly irresponsible that you couldn't help loving her. They all did, girls and governesses alike, though her fingers were always inky, and she had been born with an irre- sistible tendency to break the rules. She could never walk downstairs, she always had to jump, and the same force impelled her to shut doors with a bang, and her long black legs, under her short serge frock, were always all over the place. She would acknowledge to you openly that her chief aim in life was to do as few lessons as possible. She hadn't come to school to learn—especially French. She was always in a scrape. Somehow, her misdemeanours were committed so openly that they were invariably found out. "Oh, it is perfectly, perfectly dreadful to be leaving you all," Joyce said as she lifted her face to be kissed on the last night of her schoolgirl life. "I have been so happy here, and I love you all so much, and I just hate to think I'm going away." _ _

And she looked up to Madame with an April face of smiles shining through the tears filling her eyes, which were not laughing . then but ver j wistful. And the next day, when home-going, excited girls, and tired, cross governesses reigned over ma.dame's usually orderly household, Joyce departed in a cab amid a heap of boxes, a chattering maid and heart- broken sobs.

Monsieur and madame, after they had watched the carriage -drive away, turned with a sigh together into the house, which felt lonely to them then, for they had loved the blithe, quicksilver Joyce very much indeed, and it was sad to feel that she had gone from their lives. They hoped very earnestly that the world about which Joyce knew so little and hoped so much would prove merciful and kind to her. And in an incredibly short space of time Joyce developed into a young woman. The wavy brown hair was twisted up into a fashionable top-knot, and the impertinently short frocks were abandoned for those of more decorous diinensions. And when one day she entered Buckingham Palace in a beautiful white gown, all billowy and soft with chiffon and lace and lilies of the valley, with three feathers nodding on her pretty brown head, to make her curtsey to the Queen, she was candidly. acknowledged to be the very prettiest debatante of the season.

Seventeen was really much too young, sigho Joyce's mother, for one's first season; but then, Joyce was so eager to be launched on the big world of society, and she always got her own way in such a remarkably easy manner. And madame, in the far-away, quiet old house in the suburbs.of Paris, read an& re-read again the joyous, girlishly loving letters that came so regularly from England. "What a happy time the dear girl is having," she rewarked to monsieur. it was a very gay and fashionable party indeed that assembled at Shallowdene for Easter.

Sir Jasper and Lady Conyers arrived amid a great bustle and much rustling of her ladyship's silken skirts. As usual, she had a very great deal to say. "Ah, Joyce! My dear child, how you've grown!" she began, whilst she kissed the pretty upturned face. "So sorry I couldn't be up in town for the Drawing-R.004n. Everybody said you looked quite deliciously sweet. Jasper, this is Joyce. Come and talk to her; I want you two to be great friends, you know." And the beautiful Lady Conyers rustled off with hei society manner and her gleaming teeth to smile her sweetwt on Captain Dallas. Joyce, as Sir Jasper came up to her, lifted her big, truthful grey eyes to his. "So you are Sir Jasper! I've • 'heard such a lot about you that I almost felt ai if I knew you before; but you aren't a bit, like what I pictured you," and she almost laughed her happy, girlish laugh. "Not what you pictured me?" said Sir Jasper. "How am I different? Do tell me. Do I suffer very badly by the comparison? I hope not." . "Oh, I don't know; but you. are quite, quite different."

"Now, I believe from the way you said that I am not half so nice as you expected me to be. Tell me, Joyce, what your Jasper was like and I will try very hard to live up to him," and Sir Jasp(r's eyes, as they looked into hers, were quite grave, as if the matter were a_yery serious one indeed.

The big square hall at Shallowdene, with its sombre, old-world furniture and its bio. bowls of sweet, fresh-smelling spring flowers, echoed with the rattle of teacups and the chatter of many voices, as the flames from the wooden logs flickered and gleamed on the shining silver. There were plenty of pretty women and prettier frocks, but most brilliant among the assemblage chattered the lovely Lady Conyers. Nobody's laugh rang out quite so silvery and correctly pure in tone as hers, and nobody's teeth gleamed in quite such an even, pearly row. She was smiling at Captain Dallas with all her might. "Iteally," thought her ladyship, as she regarded him with her usual, languid gaze, which in reality was as keen, and piercing, and calculating as a hawk's, "he's about the handsomest man I ever met. Jasper looks merely commonplace beside him. That brown, leathery, Indianish look of his skin is most delightful, and such a relief after the rudely healthy, fresh-looking complexion of tho usual Briton." _ _

Captain Dallas did not turn those keen blue eyes of his on her ladyship with the open admiration which men usually displayed. It was extraordinary and somewhat tantalising that in the middle of her most bewitching and studied glance his attention seemed to wander across the room to one corner where Joyce sat, with her clear, frank eyes lifted to Sir Jasper's face, as she listened intently to what he was saying to her. After tea Joyce put on her big, picture-like hat to take Sir Jasper round to the aviary to see her doves—for Sir Jasper had suddenly grown very learned indeed about the care of doves. As they walked through the garden, down the perfectly-kept gravel walks, Sir Jasper found him- self telling this slim-figured girl all sorts of things about himself. It was good to watch her eyes fill with alarm at the story of that narrow shave with the • snake, and to see the tears well up at the account of the coolie woman's little black picaninny when the t ger carried it off into the jungle. She nev r said "Re-ally," and "Indeed," and "How awfully sad" in the sagie-tone that Lady. Conyers did. And when Joyce told him all about the school in Paris, and madame, and the Euclid classes, and the funny little old professor, Sir Jasper found all that schoolgirl history quite the most interesting conversation he had ever listened to.

At dinner her beautiful ladyship, in her gorgeous yellow satin gown, with the diamonds gleaming all over her, "which not one woman in five thousand ought. to touch," was the cynosure of all eyes, .except, perhaps, those, belonming to two men who had knocked about the world years, and who. knew a very great deal, and both of these wandered somehow to Joyce all the time—Joyce, in her simple, almost childlike chiffon frock, with not (me diamond about her, only a single •string of pearls round her slim, little white throat. It was a little bit unaccountable—and Sir Jasper, who understood most things, couldn't understand quite why, whatever was said or talked about or planned, he found himself always wondering what Joyce would think, and how Joyce would like it. Every time the door opened, when Joyce was not in the room, Sir Jasper would look up quickly, as if be expected -somebody he wanted to see very

mucn. It wasn't altogether a comfortable feeling, by any means. And once or twice Sir Jasper had felt the act that would have given him the greatest satisfaction in the world wouli have been to get up and punch the good-looking head of Captain Dallas, when that gentleman had been gazing with more than usual earnestness at a certain slip of a girl.

Lately Sir Jasper had woke up from his dr-eams, not with the remembrance of his wife's flashing eyes and rippling society laugh, but of the truthful clear grey ones, without a spice of coquetry lurking in their depths. And Joyce? Sir Jasper was not a bit, like what she had pictured him, °lily eery, very much nicer in every way. He was so big and strong and manly and handsome, and so clever, too. He knew such a vary great deal about. the world and everything, and yet he was so kind, so thoughtful, so full of chivalry. Just a man, in fact., to htt.ve in love and protect one for ever and ever. "Ah, if there could only be two Sir Jaspers in the world ! " thought Joyce. • And so the days went by, and they were very happy spring days indeed. One night, Sir Jasper sat smoking again with his friend, Captain Dallas, in the library of Shallowdene. This time it was Dick Dallas who fidgeted a little uneasily. "Jasper, old fellow, I want you to wish me all the luck that you can, for I need it badly. I haven't told you before; I couldn't talk about it even to you; but perhaps you've guessed! I'm ih love with Joyce, desperately so—clean bowled over, in fact—and I'm going to try my luck, though that she doesn't love 'me I feel perfectly sure. But she's so young, too young, in fact, to really know what love means; but if she will only give me the right, I will make her love me—l'm sure I can. I've knocked about the world, like you, a good bit, and I thought I'd got pretty well to know the sex. I fancied they were all about alike for shallowness; but Joyce—well, Joyce has taught me a lesson, and I feel grateful to Providence for letting me meet such an angel. But I'm rambling on like an idiot, though you must forgive me, Conyers—it's love, you know!" Sir Jasper's face had grown grey and drawn; there were deep lines and furrows under his eyes and round his mouth that had not been there half- an-hour ago. "You must wish me SUCC*39, old friend," went on Captain Dallas, "because your own Benedict venture has proved such a success." Sir Jasper gave a gesture of impatience, and put up one hand to shade his eyes. Then he took his friend's hand and wrung it warmly. "I do wish you joy with all my heart, Dick. Be very good to her, that's all. But you are wrong when you say that Joyce doesn't know what love means. I think she does, Dick." -

"Thanks, old fellow; and if Joyce will only give 'me the right, I'll devote the rest of my life to making her happy." Sir Jasper did not sleep that night. For hours he paced up and down his room. His brain was beating like a sledge-hammer; he could not think; he was only conscious of the utter darkness of life. And the next morning his face shewed grey and lined and haggard in the spring sunlight, and there were a few more grey hairs mixed with the rest. Her ladyship was more gay and charming and altogether fascinating than ever. She was always comfortably assured that every man in the room was in love with her; therefore she was the central figure wherever she went. She kept Captain Dallas in constant attendance upon her. He must take her for a walk right into thoFe delicious woods, where the primroses were just beginning to peep out of a yellow iarpet, and where the soft, woolly, golden balls of the willow shone out through the budding, though still naked, branches of the trees. Joyce and 'Sir Jasper gathered primroses, too. But each time the silvery tones of Lady Conyer's laugh sounded through the woods something like a shudder passed through the strong frame of Sir Jasper, for it sounded to him almost a hideous, witchlike cackle. And when at night before going down to dinner, her ladyship, in an extra gracious mood, remarked, in her condescendinc, manner: "You may kiss me if you like!" he ?eh that he absolutely loathed the beautiful, artificial face before him; lie would have liked to shake her, even to strike her—anything, in fact, to upset for a little while her complete vanity and self- satisfaction.

Coming into Sir Jasper's dressing-room late that night, with a very white look on his usually dark face, Captain Dallas said: "It is all up with me, Jasper; I've asked her, and she says she can never love me, and that I mustn't even hope. 'Pon my word, I feel now as if I'd like to take my departure of this beastly world 'altogether. What is the good of living— what's the good of anything, in fact? Good Heavens! I never thought I- could love a slip of a girl like this. To think that she won't even try to love me !" "Thank Heaven for that!" thought Sir Jasper.

div.head: BRILLIANT MARRIAGE
div.p: A BRILLIANT MARRIAGE
BY 312UTD BECKETT,
Author of "A Girton Girl," "Those Rubies,' "Child Eyes," "Eliza," "That Slip of a Girl, "A Great Heiress," &c.

Sir Jasper Conyers fidgeted somewhat uneasil3 with a paper-knife that lay on the table. He eat smoking in his cosy bachelor quarters in the Albany with his best friend, Captain Dallas, hut he was not quite happy. Round the region of his heart he felt something very like trepidation, for he had a confession to make. After a silence of some minutes, while they puffed at their weeds, he began: "Congratulate me, old fellow—l'm going to be married." Captain Dallas took the cigar from between his. teeth, and stared at him in astonishment. "Married —you, Conyers? No, not really—a confirmed old bachelor. You can't mean it," and he threw him- self back in his chair with a prolonged whistle. "It's no whistling matter, old chap—it's a perfectly serious thing; and I want you to stand by me and see me through. Will you?" "Be your best man ? Certainly I will, with the greatest pleasure in the world, Conyers; but it is a bit of a surprise for a fellow to take in all at once, you know. You're the last man in the world I should ever have thought it of; but mayn't I hear the name of•the fair lady who has succeeded in captivating the stony heart of the invulnerable Sir Jasper ?" "My dear boy, don't talk about captivating my heart, and all that sort of rot; there is no question of the tender passion in the matter at all. I've never been honestly in love in the whole course of my forty years of existence; I've got on remarkably well without it, and I shall certainly not begin the game now; but the truth is, I'm tired to death of the wandering, knockabout life I've been leading. I've visited every land on the face of the globe, and I've come to the conclusion that England's as good as any of them, and I mean to settle down. Conyers Court is running to seed for want of living in, and it's time I found a wife from somewhere to look after it. For eight months in the year I shall simmer down into a sober, respectable, fox-hunting Leicestershire squire. I'll even become their M. F. H., if they want me to, and, I'll subscribe to every local cricket club and charity bazaar the rustics like to organise." :And may you enjoy it!" interrupted his friend. "The remaining four months," continued Sir Jasper, "I'll spend in town as a regular social and domestic lap-dog ; I'll allow myself to be towed along to all the fashionable functions my wife wants to attend. I'm not quite sure how it will work out, but I'm going to try the experiment, anyhow; if it doesn't answer, we can break up the establish- ment, and her ladyship can go her way and I'll go mine, as a good many others in the world do. I want no love or tender feeling to be mixed up in the arrangement on either side; all I require of the future Lady Conyers is that she shall be good-looking enough not to disfigure the Conyers jewels and the Conyers portrait gallery; and she shall be possessed of an average share of common sense; and, above all, that she shall be a good hostess and a presentable mistress of Conyers Court. So you will see it's purely a business affair, and if the right lady hadn't turned up, I should probably have advertised for her. Fortunately, however, Miss Mabel Trefusis made her appearance in the nick of time. I met her at Lady Elphinstone's in the autumn, and later at Cannes, where we became engaged. She perfectly agrees with the terms of the bargain, and as a wife I believe she will suit me admirably. The wedding, I think, is fixed up for the beginning of March.' And then the two friends passed on to more interesting topics, and remained together talking of old times far into the night and until the first grey streaks of the dawn began to steal into the room through the folds of the half-drawn curtains. Miss Mabel Trefusis was the elder daughter of Admiral and Mrs. Trefusis, of Shallowdene, Berks, and of Park-lane. To be lovely and admired was the breath of her existence; she would have sacrificed her soul to the cause if the occasion had required. She was not quite a girl—at least, not a very young girl. She had made her curtsey to Royalty a few years before, when her sister Joyce was a little round bunch of a child in white pina- fores and a wide sash. Indeed, her real age was twenty-eight. She was quite the best-dressed woman in London—and the best-looking, too, as she would frankly acknowledge to her dearest friends, while admiring the faultless reflection of herself in one of the long mirrors in the drawing-room, with the candour which always characterised her utterances.

She had many admirers—so many, in fact, that she had ceased to count them; the wonder was that she had never been married. People marvelled at it greatly—to be beautiful, well-off, and to have passed one's ninth season in town and still remain Miss Mabel Trefusis, was the oddest thing to be sure ; but when Miss Trefusis returned to Shallowdene from Cannes, engaged to Sir Jasper Conyers, owner of fifty thousand a year, and more country houses than he knew what to do with people acknowledged amoin, themselves that the beautiful Mabel had waited to some purpose. It was a brilliant match, indeed; and then Sir Jasper was such a charming man and so handsome, too, in spite of the fact that his iron-grey hair was beginning to grow thin on his forehead. Mabel Trefusis was an exceedingly lucky woman, so the world said—and the world always knows. And the Trefiisis-Conyers wedding went off in due course with great eclat. For three days it created quite a stir arming the fashionable set who attended. Mabel Trefusis looked very beautiful—so beautiful, indeed, that Sir Jasper felt something very like pride as he walked down the aisle with his wife, and when they departed, amid an aristo- cratic shower of rice, to Snugley in the Dell, kindly lent by Lord Congleton, he remarked to himself that he had really done a wise thing in marrying the levely Miss Trefusis. _ _ _ _

At Conyers Court afterwards Lady Conyers queened it very effectually, and entirely to her own and her husband's Satisfaction. She really made a most beautiful, stately, and charming chatelaine of the solemn old oak-panelled rooms, and the celebrated Conyers rubies had never been shewn off to better advantage. "The plan works admirably," thought Sir Jasper, in his solitary moments. To his friend, Captain Dallas, in answer to a hurried note from that gentleman, he wrote.: "So .glad to have your letter, dear old fellow, and I shall be gladder still to welcome you to Conyers Court. When are you coming? Do hurry up, and make your appearance soon; your room is kept ready for you always, you know. We've got a jolly houseful here now—some pretty girls, too, among them Valentine Yorke you were .so sweet on all last season. As to the last part of your epistle, yes! a dozen :times yes, my dear boy. I find the arrangement a big success; we don't interfere with each other in the least, and Mabel is really a remarkably handsome , woman, and she does the honours of the Court in an eminently satisfactory manner; but you must really come and judge for yourself." One night, between the ,coining and going of their brilliant house parties, Sir Jasper and Lady Conyers dined alone.

Her ladyship, as she smiled at her husband across the long table, glittering with silver and glass, looked wholly brilliant, gracious, and correctly fashionable. Her gown was inimitably beautiful and appropriate, and she wore some of her exquisite diamonds. "How well you are looking to-night, Mabel !" Sir Jasper remarked, in the same level tones he would have used to .a friend in commenting on the weather.
"Yes, am I not," she answered. "Diamonds and white velvet suit me exactly ; and there's; not one woman in five thousand who ought ever to touch them."

Lady Conyers was a very clever woman, so con- seigusly so that she always said what she thought and never affected the innocent airs adopted by her weaker sisters. When they were finishing dessert she remarked : "I've just had a letter from mother by this evening's post, Jasper, and she wants me to go to Shallowdene for Easter. Joyce is coming home, you know, and I haven't seen her for ages; she must be quite grown-up now." "Who's Joyce?" asked Sir jasper, in his forgetful, well-bred way. "I've never heard of her, have I ?"

"Why, of course you have, my dear boy. I gave you her letter to read when our engagement wal announced, don't you remember? Dear little Joyce! It was too bad that she had developed those horrid, troublesome measles just at the time af the wedding. I did want her for one of my bridesmaids. Mother sent he, to Paris, you know when my old governess married and set uto

It had been a terrible accident, and altogether a very sad affair, indeed. Sir Jasper was very badly hurt—so badly, in fact, that the doctors gave little hope of his recovery. The gay crowd of visitors had all left .Shallowdene in a great hurry, for it was changed into a house of sickness now. It was strange that, after having braved so many dangers and lived through such exciting scenes, Sir Jasper should come by almost his death in such a very simple way. He had been riding through the woods with loose rein, and his horse had stumbled in a rabbit-hole and thrown him. His head had come in contact with a sharp stone, which had stunned him, and he had been drao-ged by his frightened horse for many yards, with his foot entangled in the reins, until some labourers had found him and carried him home to the frightened household, and the doctors, who were hastily summoned, said it was a very bad affair indeed, and, even though the patient might not die, it could only be a case of partial recovery. Lady Conyers promptly donned a delightfully big apron, and quite the most becoming thing in caps, an nursed him. For the time being, she was quite attntive and good-natured, but the doctors were very stupid, dried-up, old spectacled creatures, and the great house at Shallowdehe was very slow —there was simply no one to admire her; and then the deadly monotony and depression of a sick- room was bad for the complexion; and so, in a surprisingly short time, her ladyship returned to town. ,

It was very trying td Joyce to want to share the duties of the sick-room with the two entirely competent hospital nurses—they were quite enough for the most exacting of invalids, and what could Joyce know about nursing? Surely, nothing at all —only just so much as any sweet-natured, tendei- hearted woman knows how to nurse the man she loves with all the womanly goodness of her heart. Joyce, during those weeks of sickness, was very pale and very still. Joyce, who had been so gay and happy, and Laughing and mischievous, had turned into a sad- faced, wistful-eyed woman now, with always that ;Teat aching pain of hopelessness at her heart that would go on through all the long years of life that lay stretching before her. But Sir Jasper did not die; he made, instead, quite a surprising recovery; only no power on earth could save him ercin remaining a hopeless cripple all his bk. When he regained consciousness he would lie iery still, always where he could see Joyce's sweet face, as she moved about the room in her quiet, gentle way. The touch of her hand would send a thousand mad thoughts rushinft''-through his brain. One day, when he had woke up from a long and dreamless sleep—surely, he thought, that must have been a kiss he felt on his forehead.
_ Joyce was sitting by the bedside, with a tinge of carmine on her cheeks, which were always so pale now. _ _

"Ah, Joyce! i never believed in angels before, but I do now, though, for ever since I have been ill I have had one sitting by my bed! Tell me, have I been saying some very wild things lately? I am sure I am quite sane enough now, thoucji to be talked to."

- Joyce interrupted him. "I have a letter here for you, from Mabel. It calm this morning. Do you think you are well enough miw to read it yourself ?" Lady Conyers had been quite correct and regular in her correspondence since Sir Jasper had been sufficiently recovered to understand ; she had even gone so far .as tg. make her letters quite long and entertaining with all the piquant little bits of scandal about town.

But Sir Jasper did not seem anxious to open his wife's communication. Instead, lie made an angry gesture of impatience as he took the letter from Joyce's little trembling hand. "Joyce, don't talk of her ; don't let as ever mention her name between us. You know I hate and loathe and despise her, not, though, so com- pletely as I loathe and despise myself for 'making her my wife. I thought one might arrange these things to suit one's convenience. I didn't reckon with love, you see, Joyce; I had lived so long without it that I .never believed there was such a thing in the world. But since I met you my life has been so very. very chanced, and now I could

nave it m my heart to murder the hateful woman who takes away from me the right to claim your love. And, alt, Joyce, how you love me I know it, for you have let me read it in a hundred Ildlerent ways; and now what is there that HQ& before us? Nothing but just a black hapAg.tmesc Can you forgive me for blighting your young life, and for bringing you nothing but misery? Heaven grant that you can; for I cannot forgive myself. They have been happy days we have spent togethpr here at Shallowdene, though Providence has been very sparing to us, has it not? It might, I think, have granted us a little more, when it gives to some people so much. I wish I could say honestly and truthfully: 'Forget me, dear, and find some other man who will make you happy,' but I cannot, for I want you to go on loving me for ever. And what is there left to me ? 'Nothing, but to lie just a hopeless cripple dependent upon those around me for everything." "Don't—don't talk like this, for I cannot bear to hear it," interrupted Joyce, as she sank down on her knees by the bedside and buried her face in her outstretched arms.

"I said I intended to settle down at Conyers Court, ".went on Sir Jasper, with. e grim laugh, "and I shall certainly have to do so now more completely than ever I expected; only, Joyce, I shall have the blessed thought that I have known you, and shall long for you every hour of my hopeless life, and the longing will go on and on, growing more and ever more, until the merciful day. shall come When everything will vanish into a blessed, black .forgetfulness. And you, Joyce ?".
But Joyce did ii.ot answer. IV.

The lovely Lady Conyers continued to enjoy her life very much indeed. She had gathered unto herself even more admirers than ever, and each season had seemed to grow younger and more fascinating. She spent quite eight months of the year now in town, and the remaining four at her villa at Nice. Conyers Court rarely saw her; "it was so deadly dull, you know," she would remark, conversationally, to one of her admirers. And Sir Jasper, lying always there atone at Conyers Court, certainly found it very dull indeed. Sometimes, when the day was fine, he would be wheeled round to the stables, and Ladybird, his favourite hunter, would rub her soft, velvety nose against her master's coat- sleeve, and whinny inquiringly, as much as to say: "Why i.on't you mount me and let us be off ? " and Sir Jasper, patting her glossy, chestnut neck. would answer: "Ah I it's no use, Ladybird. We've had some glorious spins across country together, haven't we? But that's all over for me now."

Sir Jasper would never ride to hounds nor tramp across the turnips any more. All that was left to him to do was to lie very still all day long thinking, loving, longing for Joyce. And Joyce returned to madame's quiet house in the Rue de Bt.rmer for. a long visit. "Ah, how .completely changed!" thought madame, as she scanned the pretty, sad, wistful face before her with her keen old eyes.

,- "Deane, have you been happy since you left us? Is there anything the matter?" And Joyce answered: "Nothing, madame dear, nothing really—only I thought the world was sneh a lovely place, and instead I have found it very, very sad." [Liu END. 1

div.head: "As Ignorant as a Pig." Heavy Penalties.
div.p: "As Ignorant as a Pig." Heavy Penalties.

At Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, a case of importance affecting Friendly Societies was heard. Mr. William Long was the Chairman of the Bench,and the other magistrates present were :—Mr. Roger Parr, Colonel Ridgway, Mr. H. Nield and Mr. Joseph Knowles. The defendant was George Lythgoe, of Cross-lane Farm, Grappenhall, and the charge against him was one of receiving an amount in excess of the sum In lowed under the Friendly Societies Act, upon the death of his child, who was under five years of age. The charge in its legal phraseology was that of committing a breach of. the Friendly Societies Act. 1896, by attempting to defeat its provisions with respect to payment on the death of children under the age of five years, namely,in receiving £4 10s., a sum payable by an unregistered society known as ".The Warrington Dis- trict Children's Burial Society " in connection with the Independent Order of Oddfellows, Manchester Unity,on the death of his child, Gladys Maud Lythgoe, without production of a certificate of death containing the particulars required under Section 64 of the said Act. Defendant was also summoned for receiving an amount in eXCeS3 of the limit prescribed by the Act on the death of the said child.
In ;answer to the charge, defendant said: lam as ignorant. as a pig. (Laughter.)

-The Clerk: Do you plead guilty'or not guilty? Defendant: Guilty. The Clerk (sharply): Conduct yourself properly in Court. Don't use expressions of that kind here. Mr. Dudley Barlow, of London, solicitor to the Registrar General of Friendly Societies, prosecuted,and pointed out the provisions of the Friendly Societies Act in regard to infant life assurance. The Act provided for a certain limit in the amount to be insured on chil- dren under certain ages. The object was to prevent the over-insurance of children thatsused to be carried on and which was a great evil. It was provided in the act that a member was not allowed to draw more than a total sum of £6 upon the death of a child under fiveyears of age from all the societies in which it was insured. One of the charges against the defendant was the non-production of a certificate of death,and he (Mr. Burton) would be able to show that the production of , this certificate was the only means of checking the total amount that. was paid On the death of any child. If a child were insured in three different societies as was the case in the present instance, three separate certificates had to be issued by the Registrar. By these certificates, the representatives of the insurance societies were able to tell what amount should be paid to the defendant, r in order that the amount stipulated in the act should not be exceeded. In this case' the defendant only• obtained two certificates from the Registrar and on one of the certificates he was paid £4 10s. by the Prudential Assurance Company and on the second £1 10s. by the• General Friendly Society. That was the amount which the defendant was allowed to draw on the death of his, daughter, who was three years old. But in addition to this sum of £6 the defen- dant obtained a further sum of £4 10s. from the 'Warrington District Children's Burial Society. It appeared that the defendant and his wife went to see• the secretary of the Warrington District Children's. Burial Society to ask what payment he would receive on the death of the child. The secretary was not in but the defendant was informed that he must get a certifi- cate. When the defendant and his wife went to see Mr_ De Prez, the registrar, he informed them of the require- ments of the act and impressed upon them that the total amount they could receive in respect of the death of a. child under five years of age was £B. The defendant, although he knew be had the child insured in three societies, only asked for two certificates, and never Mentioned the third insurance. The societies themselves had no means of intera communication, and it was impossible for one society to know what insurances had been effected on the life of a single person, and it was only by means of• the issuing of a separate certificate of death for pre- sentation to each society that a cheek could be made on the amount to be paid. When the defendant went again to see the secretary of the Warrington District Children's Burial Society, lie was asked for the certifi- cate. He replied that he had forgotten to bring it, but that he would send it by post. On the representation of the defendant that a certificate had been issued, the suns pf £4 10s. was paid to the defendant. This sum was in excess of the amount allowed under the act. Mr. De Prez gave evidence as to issuing two certifi- cates to the defendant. The defendant did not ask for a third certificate nor did he mention that he had the- child insured in three societies. Witness explained to the defendant and his wife that they could only receive on the death of the child. • The Secretary of the Warrington District Children's Burial Society also gave evidence. The defendant told him that his wife had the certificate at home, and he would go to fetch it. it was a wet night and as the defendant promised to send the certificate by post, wit-. ness paid him £4 10s. On the following dayhe received • a doctor's certificate and not a registrar's certificate. The Defendant: I did not know about this new act which only allowed £0 to be drawn. • Mr. Barlow: The act was passed in 1875, Sir. The Clerk: Youknew that you had drawn .£4 10s. too. much.
The Defendant: I would not have had it if I had known.
The Clerk: You have had it some Considerable time. The Defendant: T did not know anything about it. The Chairman: What were you paying to these societies?

The Defendant: I was paying twopence a fortnight. My wife was paying into the other two societies. The chairman: You must have paid a. goad many twopences, and yet you kncw you could only draw £6 at death.

The Bench retired to consider their decision. On returning into Court the Chairman said the Bench were unanimously of opinion -that this was a very bad case indeed. There was no knowing the danger that was. done by these sort of cases—the insuring of children for larger sums than the parent was allowed to draw. The object of the Government in making this law was that children should not be insured for more than a certain sum. The defendant had stated that he did not .know anything about it. but it was his duty to have known. They would mark their sense of the case very strongly. The defendant would be fined including costs on the first charge and £3 and costs on the second..

div.head: Social,
div.p: Social,

The members of th'-‘ choir of tip ( Thirch of the- Sacred Heart had their annual social in the school- room on Tuesday evening. The attendance numbered between thirty and forty, and included, in addition to the members of the choir, several invited friends. An excellent ssupper was prepared by Mrs. J. Gibtins, assisted. by Misses Davies, Johnson, Fairclough and Eastens. After supper a musical programme was gone through, Mr. J. Broadbent being an efficient accompanist The Rev, Father Ryan was present. Mr. J. Gibbons thanked the choir for their services, and said that if they continued their practice they would become very efficient. He mentioned the fact that at the Warrington Eisteddfod, the choir made 80 marks out of a possible 100, which, he thought, was very creditable.

THE INSTALLATION OF THE ARC:
EEK.
P AT WESTMINSTER.
A FAMOUS LONDON BUILDING.

Perhaps the most interesting building to suffer demolition in the course of the Strand to Holborn improvements is the historical chapel in Little Wild Street. This quaint old building is very conspicuous in history. In the early part of the reign of Charles I. the site of Little Wiid Street was known as Oldwick Close, and on it Sir Edward Stradling built himself a house with a frontage of 150 feet and a depth behind with the garden of 300 feet—a lordly town dwelling. The house was sold in 1651 to Humphrey Weld, son of Sir Hum- phrey Weld, Lord Mayor in 1608. From the Welds the house was thereafter so named, Wild being a subsequent corruption. The Weld family (of Lul- worth Castle, Dorset) seem to have always let the

THE OLD CHAPEL IN LITTLE WILD STREET. LONDON, SHORTLY TO BE DEMOLISHED. house to personages of importance. The Duchess of Ormond was living in it in 1655, and the Spanish Ambassador, Ronquillo, was there in the time of the second Charles and James. The next record we have of Wild House is a notice in the "London Gazette," 1694, that it was "to be lett," and that it contained thirty-three rooms, garrets and cellars, with other suitable conveniences. In the follow- ing year the house and gardens were let on a building lease for ninety-nine years, and the pre- sent—soon to be the past—thoroughfares of Great and Little Wild Street were built upon the site. Of late years the chapel has been used as the hall of the St. Giles's Mission. In this chapel was held the annual "Thieves' Supper," and in bygone days the minister of the chapel always preached a sermon in commemoration of the great storm of 1703, which caused such tremendous damage and loss of life that the memory of it remained for generations. Winstanley and his fantastic Eddy- stone Lighthouse perished in that tempest, and it was estimated that 8,000 people were killed, drowned in the floods, or lost at sea. Beneath the chapel are said to lie the remains of no fewer than 600 human beings—some of them within a yard of the floor.

div.head: NEW ARCHBISideP.
div.p: THE NEW ARCHBISideP.

The Archbishop of Canterbury has been thely Installed as Primate upon his return from the Continent, whither he went to recruit his health directly after his nomination by the King. The -ceremony took place at the Church Muse, West- minster, and finally places Dr. Randall Davidson in full possession of the See of Canterbury after the various forms of nomination and election, which have to be complied with. The Archbishop of York presided, and was supported by the Bishops of Bath and Wells, Chichester, Ely, Exeter, London, Salisbury and Worcester. Amongst those present in their official capacities were the Vicar-General Viir. C. A. Cripps. K.C.), the Chancellor of the Diocese of London (Dr. Tristram), the Apparitor- General (Sir John Hanham), and Mr. H. Lee. the Registrar-General; while gathered in the Great Hall was a large number of prominent persons, including the Earl of Rosebery. Before joining the general meeting the Bishops sat in conclave to receive any objections to the confirmation of the Arabishop-Elect, if any had been made, but it was 'notified that none had been received, and at eleven 'o'clock they enteted the Great Hall, headed by the Archbishop of York. They all wore their robes of Convocation; and, as Prelate of the Garter, the Archbishop-Elect wore the ribbon and badge of the Order. The proceedings opened by the reading of the Royal Letters constituting the Court, and then the Bishop of Salisbury sang the litany. The report of the election of Dr. Randall Davidson by the Dean and Chapter of Canterbury was then read, and after it His Majesty's approval of their choice. Next Sir John Hanbam, as Apparitor-General, called upon any who wished to oppose the election to do so. but met with nc response. Thereupon-the Archbishop-Elect knelt and took the oath of fealty, and the Archbishop of York promulgated the confirmation of the election, which was signed by the other Bishops. Then the newly confirmed Archbishop of Canterbury brought the proceedings to a close by pronouncing the Benediction. Subsequently Dr. Davidson went -down to Windsor to kiss hands upon his appoint- ment, and stayed at the Castle over the week-end, predching on Sunday morning. Few recent ceremonies in the Church of late years have passed off so harmoniously, and it is plain that the choice of Dr. Randall Davidson as successor to Dr. Temple has given general satisfaction.

div.head: UNEMPLOYED.
div.p: THE UNEMPLOYED.

One of the most common features of Landon life at the moment are the daily processions of the unemployed through the principal thoroughfares; and, it may be added, one of the chief subjects of criticism. The general opinion abroad is that only Binall proportion of those who tramp with the ."•rious bodies, each identified by its separate
flhll_ i.:11r1
(TORS
FOR MANY WEEKS NOW, LARGE BODIES OF UNEMPLOYED MEN HAVE PARADED LONDON STREETS.

banner, are genuine labourers out of work, whc caTmot get a job. Certainly there is a strong leavening of "no-workers," as the police call them and thus sympathy is distracted from the bond Ifidi cases. Indeed, the collection boxes, shaken pro. misouously in everyone's face, and the none toc courteous demands for money are becoming a public nuisance of the gravest type. Arms are thrust into carriages and cabs, omnibuses are invaded wholesale, and pedestrians are literally "stuck up." Yet the distress in London is nc worse than in previous years, the season is lest inclement than its wont, and the state of the labour market is much the same as usual, Thu' this new feature of London life, which looks aE though it has come to stay, and finds resulti Profitable enough to justify existence, is hard tc understand. Hitherto the various processiont have been very well behaved, but here credit if especially due to the police, who are careful tc preserve the strictest of law and order and tc prevent any signs of rowdyism—to say nothing of the public generosity. In fact, the conduct of Om police throughout, their good nature and well. organised firmness, reflect the greatest credit on the force. London, however, is growing tired ol these perpetual parades and. this continuous im. portunity, and them is no doubt that, unless it shortly dies a natural death, it will be put down b 3 the authorities. Nothing has done more harm to:: the cause of labour or has alienated more sympathy for many years. and the pity of it is that such large percentage of the men, who are only doing harm to a good cause, are themselves obviously confirmed loafers.

div.head: ESPINGOLE DISASTER.
div.p: THE ESPINGOLE DISASTER.

The French Navy has suffered a disaster in th( loss of thg,destroyer Espingole, which is reported to have foundered after striking a rock off „Cap( Lardier in the Mediterranean, and she will prove s considerable loss to our Gallic neighbours, as it if

only two years since she was built, and she was one of the best of her class across the Channel. However, as no lives were lost, and considering the recent utterances of the French Minister of Marine, it would be very superficial politeness for us to express great sympathy with the French Navy in their loss. The Espingole carried a crew of forty-five officers and men, who all fortunately escaped to tell the tale and the only loss was that of the boat herself. She had a displacement of 303 tons, and carried seven guns, one 9-pounder and six 3-pounders. She also carried two torpedo- tubes which, with the guns were mounted on a sort Of flying deck, which is usual in French boats of this class, but not seen in English ones. This flying deck, which is of great use in bad weather, is a superstructure over the whole length of the destroyer at some considerable height above the upper deck, which would otherwise generally be awash in a heavy sea. The Espingde had a maximum speed of twenty-seven knots, and curie tbirty-eight tons of coal.
THE ESPINGOLE, THE LOST FRENCH DESTROYER.

div.head: GREAT AMERICAN SOLDIER.
div.p: A GREAT AMERICAN SOLDIER.

The Commander-in-Chief of the United States irmy, has been amongst our recent visitors, and he received a special mark of royal favour i the shape of a" dine and sleep" invitation to Windsor Castle upon the occasion of Sousa's band playing before the King. The King, it will be remembered, paid the States the great compliment of rising personally when the" Star-Spangled Banner" was played, and part of this compliment was undoubt- edly directed to General Nelson A. Miles, who ill no stranger either to England or royalty, as he was one of the representatives of the States at Queen Victoria's Jubilee in 1887. This visit, however, he was here in an entirely private capacity, staying only a few days on his way home on a voyage round the world, and the invita- tion to Windsor was a purely personal on e. When General Miles was over here in 1887, he made a close study of our Army, its method, its fac- tories and its GENERAL MILES, arsenals. The COMMANDER-IN-CHIEF OF VIP history of his life UNITED STATES ARMY. is a most roman- tic and inter- esting one—one of those cases of truth surpassing fiction. When the Civil War broke out, he was a boy behind a counter ; but before its close at the age of twenty-three he had fought his way up step by step to he rank of tuajo-general and was covered with !-_,iory and scam Then he turned his attention to fighting the Indians, the Apaches, the Cheyennes and other taibes, and his experiences against the coloured men of the prairies and back- woods were most vatied and brilliant. Next he headed, the American troops in the Chicago riots, and then lie led the Army in the war against Spain. His has, indeed, been a distinguished career, and he stands quite at the head of his pro- fession in the States.
CAPE MOUNTED RIFLES AND NINTH LANCERS.

The eye of the public has been focussed upon till 9th Lancers upon many occasions during the last three years, and the greatest sympathy has been expressed for them in their present trouble. The regiment, it will he remembered, is in disgrace in India, and, to a man, under arrest, so to speak, being confined to barr:lcks with all leave stopped. This collective punishment of a gallant regiment is the drastic measure of Lord Curzon, who has not

THE HANDSOME ~NTREPIECE PRESENTED BY THE C.M.R. TO THE 9TH LANCERS IN MEMORY OF FRIENDSHIP FORMED DURING THE WAR. added to his popularity by it. His object was to punish the undiscovered murderer of an Indian cook, who was found beaten to death within their lines. This is much to be regretted, if only for the fact that no regiment did better out in South Africa than the 9th Lancers. Much of their work was done in company with the Cape Mounted Rifles, and between the two the best of good fellowship prevails. On the principle of "a frien4 in need" the C.M.R. have taken the opportunity or showing their friendship at this trying time by the presentation to the regiment of a massive PUT= bowl.

div.head: Examiner, Friday, February 13,1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Friday, February 13,1903.
OLDHAM v. WIGAN.

I These teams met at Watersheddings, before a small attendance. S. Lees was enabled to land a goal from a penalty. Fora time play fluctuated, and after Bothwell had narrowly missed equalising, the Oldham forwards rushed the oval over, and J. H. Wilkinson scored an unimproved try. Quite a change came over the game soon after. Thomas let the visitors take up a good position, and Barr scored at the corner twice in quick succession. Towards the interval, Oldham rushed the ball down to Wigan's line, and Brady scored behind the posts. Sam Lees failed at goal. Half-time score : Oldham 1 goal 2 tries (8 points), Wigan 2 tries (6 points). Oldham resumed, and some smart play was seen. From a passing bout Spottiswoode was served, and beating the full back, scored at the corner. Another brilliant exhibition by the Oldham backs saw Cash score at the opposite corner, and Oldham won by 1 goal,' tries 11 points), to Wigan 2 tries (6 points).
BROUGHTON RANGERS v. HUNSLET : A CLEVER YORKSHIRE WIN.

Although the weather was miserably wet and cold in Manchester, there was a crowd of some 3,000 people at \Theater's Field to see the return game between Broughton Rangers and Hunslet. Hunslet played against the wind in the first half, and by means of vigorous forward play fully held their own in the opening stages. The Rangers opened the scoring, James placing a fine goal. This was the only score up to half-time. In the second half Hunslet showed clever generalship on several occasions when Broughton got to close quarters, but James again lowered their goal from a penalty kick. Near the close, at a time when the home side were at full strength, Walter Goldthorpe followed up cleverly and tackled Fielding near his line. The ball came out of the succeeding scrummage on the Hunslet side, and J. Whiteley slipping in before his opponents had time to realise his intentions picked up and dodged past Hampson, scoring a grand try. From a by no means easy place Albert Goldthorpe kicked a fine goal. Broughton struggled desperately to regain the lead, but found the Hunslet defence too sound for them, and the shield holders retired beaten by a point—a goal and a try to two goals.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION LEAGUE. -The Huddersfield Ground Suspended.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION LEAGUE. -The Huddersfield Ground Suspended.

A meeting of the Northern Union League Committee was held at the Exchange Hotel, Manchester, on Tues- day night, Mr. R. Collingo (Rochdale) presiding. The first item on the agenda was the consideration of the resignation of Mr. Ernest Gresty, the well-known Broughton Rangers representative, and one of the lead- ing and hardest working officials in the Union. Mr. Gresty has been obliged to take this step owing to indifferent health, coincident with pressing business claims, and his resignation was accepted with regret. The most important business, however, was the con- sideration of the report made by the Salford Club on the conduct of the Huddersfield spectators after the match on January 31. Evidence was adduced to prove that hostile demon- stration had been made, and missiles thrown at the conveyance containing the Salford players and officials. After a lengthy and patient hearing, it was decided to suspend theßuddersfield ground up to and including February 28th, and the Committee further ordered the- Huddersfield and Oldham match fixed for that date to be played at Halifax. Another match in which the Salford Club was con- cemed,related _to Altrincham having broken their en- gagement with the complaining club on October 25th. The Committee decided that Altrincham be mulcted in a sum of El. 10s., which will be awarded to the Salford Club out of the proceeds of the cup-tie between the clubs concerned on Saturday, subject to approval by the Cup Committee. The explanations of A. Lee and C. Abraham, officials in matches at Runcorn and Millom respectively, the first named for late arrival and the latter for non-attendance were accepted. Sanction was given to the alteration of the Hebden Bridge v. Wakefield Trinity A match on the first-named ground from February 7 to March 21. , The following players were reported and dealt with: ' —Ridsdale, Brighouse Rangers, foul language, suspended to February 21; Wade, Saville, Green and Lewis, Hall A, striking, suspended till February 21 and 14 respectively Liddimore, Keighley, kicking, February 14; Meeson, Dewsbury, kicking' February 21. Dalton, of Castleford, who. had been suspended for a fortnight for striking,was reinstated from dat% SWINTON'S APPEAL: RESOLUTE NEGATIVE.

A meeting of the General Committee of the Northern Union was held at the Exchange Hotel, Manchester, on Tuesday evening, Mr. J. Clifford presiding. The South Shields St. Paul's P.C. were fined a guinea for failure to send in cup-tie register, and it was ordered that the same should be forwarded at once. The resignation of Mr. E. Gresty, of the Broughton Rangers Club, as was the case at the Northern League meeting, was received with regret. The committee instructed the Secretary to convey to him the high appreciation they had of .the very valuable services he had rendered, and also their great pleasure in learning of his restoration to health. Fred Goodfellow, of Holbeck, who was suspended sine die by the Northern Union in December, 1901, for breach -of professional laws, applied for reinstatement. It was resolved that Goodfellow be reinstated from March 1, next. The Lancashire County Football Union was granted a sum of £5O to be disbursed in support of junior football. _ _

The Swinton Club wrote asking that the case of T. Samuels be re-opened. The Committee decided against the application on the ground that the breach was so clear,that o nly the finding already given could be re- affirmed, and adopted the reply showing the ruling upon the points raised. The arrangement with the English Association was confirmed as follows:- 1. The Football Association and the Northern Rugby Union mutually agree to recognise each other's suspen- sions. 2. Penalties apply to.clubs and players alike. 3. Any club or player suspended by either authority, shall be suspended by the other for a period of twelve months. 4. Neither authority claims any jurisdiction over the clubs that are players of the other who have resigned,or may hereafter resign, before committing any breach of the rules for which punishment might be awarded. A professional player of one authority shall not be entitled to play for the other as an amateur, nor shall a pro- fessional player of one authority play under the auspices 'of the other during the same season. 5. The secretary of each authority agrees to send to the other, lists of suspensions and expulsions. 6. In the event of either secretary informing the other that a suspended player is playing according to his code, it is hereby agreed to prevent such player from continuing to play. 7. The authorities also agree to prevent a club under one authority taking a name identical with that already held under the other authority. The Manningham Club was fined 10s. for breach of Professional Law 1, Sub-section C, in respect of F. Lorriruan. The Eel's United Club were also fined 10s. for a breach of the same rule. The Committee decided to draw the second round of the cup ties in three districts, as follows :-1. Lanca- shire (north of Preston), Cumberland and Westmorland. 2 Lancashire (south of Preston), Cheshire. 3. York- shire and Durham. The Committee decided to allow finalists the same expenses as last year. The following rulings were given : Is a referee right in penalising a half back who attempts to put the ball in the scrummage, but draws back, thus causing forwards to put their feet up? Answer: Yes.

Is it legitimate for a half back to bounce or throw the ball into a scrummage with a downward motion or in- fluence, instead of underhand. Answer: The Commit- tee decided that the matter was one in which it would be unwise to give a ruling. The question of fair putting inmustbe left entirely with the referee.

div.head: Public Health.
div.p: The Public Health.

The Registrar-General reports that the annual rate of mortality last week in the seventy great towns of England and Wales averaged 17-9 per 1,000. The rate in Birkenhead was 18, Wallasey 16, Liverpool 23, Bootle 22, St. Helens 15, Wigan 23, Warrington 17, Preston 24, and Barrow-in-Furness 12.

Anticipations Realized. "It will only be a month for me. It will get the winter ovei• " said Thomas Smith, of Ship-yard, when he was being taken to the Police Station on Monday afternoon by Constables Clough and Edwards for begging in Bridge-street. Clough saw the man stop three gentlemen, and in an impudent manner, ask them for coppers towards his lodging money.--Prison- ers' 'anticipations in regard to the penalty for his mis- doings were realized, the magistrates on Tuesday morning sentencing him to a mouth's hard labour. Hunting. On Saturday the North Cheshire Hunt met at Dutton Hall Farm, when there was a big field. A good 25 minutes' hunt was enjoyed from Whitley Gorse. Rey- nard ran within a field of Gobler's Gorse, then past Stretton Church tolGrimsditch, making a ring back to Dutton Hall Farm, where he got to ground. Dutton Dingle and Newton were blank, and a brief hunt fol- lowed from Rose Wood. The scent was interfered with by a storm which came on in the afternoon. A fox was viewed at Appleton Firs, but nothing was made of him.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION. THE LEAGUE.---FIRST DIVISION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION. THE LEAGUE.---FIRST DIVISION.

WARRINGTON v. SALFORD. The second meeting of the season between these two teams came off at Warrington on Saturday before 4,000 people. Unfortunately for the prospects of the homesters, they were without Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Burgess, the backbone of the team. In their places lappeared Knight, Foster' and Edmunds, Hockenhall I going into three-quarter. On the other hand, Salford played their strongest team with the exception of I Preston. The ground was in a sodden condition.—Mr. I Squires, Broughton, was the referee, and the players were as follows :

Warrington—Hallam, back; Forster, Hockenhall, Kni,ght, and Harris, three-quarter backs; Duckworth wad Edmunds, half backs; Morrison, Boardman, Naylor, Edmondson, Ashton, Farmer, Roberts, and Warburton, forwards.

Salford—Smith, back; Norris, Messer, Bell,and Riley, three-quarter backs; Lomas and Harter, half backs; Rhapps, Tunney, Heath, Williams, R. Shaw, H. Shore, Buckler' and Brown, forwards. Roberts kicked off for Warrington against a strong wind. For offside play a scrimmage was ordered. Lomas got away well, .and passed to Messer, and he to Bell, who was promptly floored by Knight. Lomas next took a penalty kick, which, however, was not successful, Foster touching down. Another incursion by Salford, who were helped by the wind, also ended in a dead ball. Immediately after the drop out Knight intercepted one of Lomas's passes, and kicked over Smith's head. Hockenhall tried to secure the ball, but Norris just beat him and kicked in touch. From the 'next scrimmage the ball was sent over the Salford line, but Smith touched down. The depleted Warrington team were play- ing up splendidly, and for a time penned Salford in their quarters. A good dribble by Bell regained Salford lost ground, and Hallam did well in keeping him out. War- rington were now hard pressed, but tackled desperately, Knight in particular distinguishing himself. At length good forward play gotthe ball to safer quarters. Riley, however, got clear away, and appeared to have a clear run behind the posts, but Harris held him up on the line. Norris was knocked into touch at the corner the next minute. Warrington, however, could not keep Salford out, and a cross kick by Lomas caught them napping, as it enabled Williams to force his way over the line, Lomas failing at goal. Play now quietened down, and was for the greater part of the time in the Warrington half. Lomas made a good opening for Messer, and the latter was racing down at full speed when Edmunds succeeded in flooring him. From now until the interval Salford almost continually pressed, but met with a stubborn defence, and when half-time I arrived the teams were at mid-field. Half-time: ' Salford, 1 try; Warrington, nil. Lomas re-started, but the ball went in touch. Hocken- hall dribbled down the field, and Edmunds and Hallam supplemented by kicks in touch, which gained consider- able ground. The play was very interesting, and was chiefly in midfield. At length. passing between Duck- worth, Edmonds, and Harris, followed by a kick by the latter, put Warrington in a good position. Smith did not clear his line very well, and severaLsevere scrim- mages took place on the quarter-line, and Warrington got within measurable distance from the Salford goal- posts. A good chance came to Foster from a pass by Duckworth, but he failed to hold the ball. Soon after- wards Duckworth stole away from a scrimmage and kicked into touch close to the corner.—Harmer made his mark, and Knight kicked a goal from a very difficult angle. With one point only between the teams, play became much more exciting, and Hockenhall was prominent with a dribble which gained a large amount of ground. A dangerous dribble by the Salford for- wards almost ended in disaster for Warrington, Hallam and Knight saving in daring fashion. Riley intercepted a pass intended for Duckworth, and almost got clear, Hallam just knocking him in touch in time. The Salford forwards again forced their way to centre, but Edmunds got hold and passed across. Bell intercepted and getting off well ran clean from the ce,ntre and scored, Lomas kicking a goal. This completely settled Warrington's chances, just when they looked like getting ahead. Salford now overplayed the homesters and Messer scored after good passing, the final being: Salford,l goal 3 tries (11 points).; Warrington, 1 goal (2 points).

div.head: RUNCORN v. ST. HELENS
div.p: RUNCORN v. ST. HELENS

The return match was pla.Yed at Irwell-lane on Satur- day, there being only a moderate attendance. Farmer opened for Runcorn against a strong wind. From the first scrimmage Jolley gained possession, and the ball was sent from Richardson to Butterworth and on to Price, who gave to Moran, and a try was scored in the first minute at the top corner. Farmer failed from a difficult angle. The visitors' defence was severely tested, but held out well. Richardson offered Butterworth a splendid opportunity, but he misfielded the ball. The visiting forwards now gained possession, and Banks and Hall topped the effort with a smart bott of passing The "Saints were penalizey at the home quarter-line but maintained the aggressive, until Price came through with a splendid run and passed to Moran, who sprinted past Foulkes and scored behind the posts. Farmer had no difficulty in adding the extra points. The visitors were still kept upcn the defensive. Richardson received in his own" twenty-five," and brushing aside all opposi- tion ran in a splendid try at the corner and Farmer improved the score with a magnificent kick. Nothing daunted by these repeated reverses, the visitors played most pluckily, and by the aid of excel- lent kicking once again invaded the Runcorn territory but their stay-was a brief one,. Houghton and Butter- worth sending them. to the right about. Richardson bluffed several opponents, but:eventually found his man, and play was in mid-field when half-time came with the score, Runcorn, two goals and three tries; St. Helens, nil. Resuming, Butterworth made a grand attempt to break through, and then a passing movement resulted in Moran notching his third try. The kick for goal failed. Wareing and Bacon ran well along the touch, and Houghton was called upon. He responded with an ex- cellently judged kick to touch, and thereafter the homesters made a strong but abortive effort to break through. The visiting forwards gained ground with a dribble, but Houghton changed the venue of play. Un- interesting play followed. Moran was foully charged. Farmer had a shot for goal but missed badly. The visi- tors were mostly in possession, but could gain no tangible result against the excellent defence of the homesters. Jolley essayed akick for goal which failed. The home backs now passed well, and negligence on the part of Butterworth denied Jones of two excellent opportunities. Before the close Moran scored cleverly, but the kick for goal failed. Runcorn ran out winners by two goals and five tries to nothing. HULL V. WIDNES. •

Played on the Hull Boulevard Ground, before a saml attendance. Hull won the toss, and Widnes started against the wind, and it was from a bit of fine play by Taylor that the first points were scored. After saving a rush, he gave to Ellerington, who raced through a quartette of opponents and placed the ball over the line. HarrisOn made an erratio and futile shot for goal, and the half-time score stood at 3 points to nil. After the interval Frank made a grand display, and ,by dashing through the ranks of Widnes and doubling to the wing he was ableto transfer to Cook at a favourable moment. The latter player passed to .Moxon,who simply strolled. in. Taylor's kick failed. Soon afterwards some very sraart passing enabled Parry to score, and the goal was added by Wade, the game ending :—Hull 1 goal and 3 tries (11 points), Widnes nil. Teams : Hull: Taylor, back; Moxon Cook, Morgan, and Parry, three-quarter backs; Frank and Goddard, half backs ; Wade, Harrison, Longhorn, Fulton. Ellerington, Spenoeley, Rhodes, and John, forwards. Widnes: Tilley, back; Waling, Whelan, Peacock, and Hughes: three-quarter backs; Lally and Taylor, half backs • McDon:ld, Riley, Power, Leyston, Lynch. Webster, Rigby, and Cockeram. forwards. Referee. Mr. W. Lancaster (Rochdale). Touch judges, Messr3. W. Emmott (Les) and M. Carr (Hunslet).

div.head: LEIGH v. BRADFORD.
div.p: LEIGH v. BRADFORD.
At Leigh before 2,000 people. Both sides missed chances of scoring, and though Leigh held a big advan- tage forward they could only draw. There was no score.

div.head: BATLEY v. BRIGHOUSE.
div.p: BATLEY v. BRIGHOUSE.
Brighouse Rangers were at Batley on Saturday, and made a good fight. Hodgson kicked a goal for the homesters, and Saville equalised for Brighouse,the game ending in a draw of 2 points each.

div.head: SWINTON v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.
div.p: SWINTON v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.

The attendance at Swinton for this match was only of moderate dimensions. Cards and Morfitt at half back were more than match' for Morgan and William- son, and outwitted them on-many occasions. Again the Rovers' forwards held the master hand, and Swinton were somewhnt lucky to escape defeat. They might have won, however, almost on time, fof Preston. failed miserably from a penalty., The game ended without anything being scored.

div.head: HALIFAX v. HUDDERSFIELD,
div.p: HALIFAX v. HUDDERSFIELD,

This return mntch was played at Halifax, before an. • attendance much below the average. Huddersfield had to play against the wind in the first half, and they were on the defence for the greater part of the time. Within five minutes from the st,art the Halifax forwards dribbled in a body to the line, and Kitson grounded the ball ins fairly easy position. Little kicked a goal. Halifax continued to have the advantage, and Brown was once nearly over. Little ultimately kicked a penalty goal, and a little later he was nearly successful with another shot, the ball striking the uprights and rebounding into play. Result :—Halifax 2 goals and I try (7 points), Huddersfield nil. .

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
A POINTLESS DRAW AT SALFORD.

A pointless draw was the result of Warrington " A's" encounter with Salford A" on the Weaste enclosure on Saturday. Shawstarted, and Salford at once pressed, Clare marking in defence. Fletcher put in a good run, but a free kick to Ratcliffe found touch at centre, and Warrington came into the home half, Hignett even* tually conceding a dead ball. The heavy state of the ground spoiled back play, although Hunter put in a fine ran, only to slip when all opposition had been cleared. Fletcher and Walsh for Salford, and Bailey for the visi- tors were prominent in subsequent play in which War- rington had the advantage for a time, Hignett being tackled with the ball, and Bollaud kicking dead. Resuming, Salford took up the attack, whilst Ratcliffe, from a mark, and later Bailey, removed play to the home line, where Shore effected some relief. A combined run by Brooks and Watkins placed Salford on the defence, but a free kick to Shaw cleared. Warrington were not to be shaken off, and Salford had again to save. Clare dropped fruitlessly at goal, another dead ball accruing. Shore ran well for Salford, but Warrington replied to half way. Salford recovered themselves for a few minutes,until the visitors came again, Shaw saving and Shore running to centre. Half-time: No score. ,The second half was characterized by a succession of scrambling rallies, in which the advantage generally rested with the visitors, and some kicking exchanges from which Salford gained ground. Result: Salford "A," nil ; Warrington "A," nil.

div.head: ASSOCIATION. THE COMBINATION. MIDDLEWICII V. NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS
div.p: ASSOCIATION. THE COMBINATION. MIDDLEWICII V. NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS

At Middlewich, in rough weather. Newton kicked off and for some time play was in midfield. Then the visitors attacked, but were repulsed by a strong defence. The -Middlewich left wing got dovvn,and Moss shot past the post. The strong wind spoiled accurate play, and the ball was frequently outside. Jenkinson saved a good shot from Moss,and at the opposite end Morse shot wide. Half-time: Middlewich nil, Newton-le-Willows, nil. Final: Middlewich 1, Newton nil. LANCASHIRE LEAGUE. E AntEsTowN v.' DA RWEN.

Played at Earlestown on Saturday in miserable weather. Earlestown were short of Martin and Limond, Bartley and Pennington coming into the team, the visitors being at full strength. Da.rwen lost the toss, and Bartley set the ball in motion against the hill in the presence of a mere handful of spectators. The home left were early prominent, but Haslam neatly robbed Leach when; the latter was nicely situated. A rush to the other end resulted in Kirkbright shooting yards wide. Tricky work by Leach and Barlow enabled the former to get a long shot, which Hill easily cleared. A promising move by the visitors' left was splendidly stopped by Leigh, and in a trice the leather was at the other end. AToul against the visitors close in looked , ominous, but Haslam got the leather away in line style. At this point Goulding turned out and completed the home eleven. From a penalty against Cottam, Hinks opened the visitors' account. In a collision with Bart ley Haslam the visitors' right back,broke his collarbone Half-time—Darwen 1, Earlestown nil. Final: Darwen 1, Earlestown nil.

div.head: NATIONAL FREE lIHURCH COUNCIL,
div.p: NATIONAL FREE lIHURCH COUNCIL,

The General Committee of the National Council of the Evangelical Free Churches met at the Memorial Hall, London this week. The President Rev. W. J. Townsend D.D. occupied the chair. There was a large attendance of representatives from all parts of the country. The Rev. F. R. Meyer, 8.A., by a standing vote was unanimously nominated as President for 1904-1905. It is probable the annual Council for 1994 will be held either at Newcastle-on-Tyne or Manchester. Rev. J. Monro Gibson, D.D. presented a report of the visit of Rev. J. F. B. Tinling, M.A., to Canada. During Mr. Tinling's visit he addressed a large number of meetings in the interest of the Free Church Federation movement.

The organizing report was presented by the Rev. Thomas Law, who stated that 66 new Councils had been formed during the year covering suoh towns as Faring- don, Congleton, Chelmsford, Brentwood, Faversham, Alton, Ramsey, Hertford, Bishops Stortford, Sidcup, Prestwich, Sleaford, Hunstanton, Pembroke Dock, New Mill, Ardsley and Ripponden. Among the Councils formed during the last few weeks are Kilkhampton, Bude and District, Hertford, Bishops, Stortford, Alton, Chiswick, Sidcup, Winchmore Hill, Harwich, Padiham, Prestwich, Sidgeford, Quarry Bank, Langley, Abergele, Taff's Well, Ardsley, Worsborough Dale, Ripponden, Mytholmroyd and Nathallerton.

Mr. Law also reported that the Federation Movement is rapidly developing abroad, communications are con- stantly received at the Central Office, Memorial Hall, with reference to the work; the latest councils being that at Hobart, _Southern Tasmtmia.
New Federations have just been formed for Herefore- shire and Essex. These District Federations now cover every county in England and also North and South Wales.

The report of the Girls' Guild shews there are now 160 branches. Permanent Homes have been opened at Cardiff, Halifax, Cheltenham, Chatham, Maidstone, Sydenham and Forest Hill. All classes of girls are be- ing reached and most of the Guilds arrange for nursing lectures—some of whichare conducted by qualified lady doctors. The Girls' Guild Topics and Lantern Lectures have been well used. Members and associates now number nearly 10,000. Mr. Law further reported with regard to the Educa- tion Campaign that further steps were being taken, and that the National Council and all the local Councils throughout the country were fully alert.

WORLD'S COALING RECORD.—At Portsmouth on Wed- nesday, H.M.S. Mars made a world's coallbg record. She took aboard 1,570 tons, at an average rate of a fraction above 241 tons per hour. This is a great advance upon the record of 212 tons per hour estab- lished by H.M.S. Majestic a few weeks ago. The Mars has always been noted for expeditious coaling, and generally stands at the head of the fleet in this evolution. Fined at West Ham on Wednesday for being in unlaw- ful possession of tobacco, a man employed at Victoria Docks complained that he hadnot robbed anyone except the " King's pipe."

TRADE I JANUARY.—Front the Board of Trade returns for January, it appears that the imports to this country for that month reached £46,226,515,a decrease on the corresponding month of last year of £3,915,833 or 8.46 per cent, while the exports amounted to £24,903,636 showing an increase of £634,462, or 2.54 per cent. The exports of foreign and Colonial merchandise were valued at £6,067,718, and were 11.98 per cent. over those of the first month of 1902.
