OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was a well-attended meeting in connection with this society on Sunday afternoon in Wycliffe Church. Mr. B. Farrar presided and delivered a few encouraging remarks based on the words "Let go." He appealed to his hearers to endeavour to lead good lives, and influence others by consistency of conduct.—Mr. Wat- son, of Liverpool, delivered the address, and spoke upon the benefits to be derived from public worship.—Miss Allen, of Earlestown, sang two solos entitled " Daddy" and" The Heavenly Song."—Mr. F. Brown led the devo- tional part of the service.

Temperance Services at Cockhedge Mission. Services in connection with Wycliffe (Cockhedge) _Congregational Band of Hope were held in the Mission on Sunday. The superintendent of the Sunday School (Mr. Andrew Scriven) addressed the scholars in the morning. Basing his remarks on the words "And this also we wish, even your perfection." Ile warned his hearers to take great precaution against the evils of in- temperance, urging upon them total abstinence as a mighty aid to their future welfare. In the afternoon a meeting was held, presided over by Mr. Scriven. An address was given by the Rev. Herbert Dunnico upon "Is life worth living?" and Mr. George Whitfield delighted the congregation by the manner in which he delivered two recitations upon the temperance subject. Mr. W. Light was the preacher for the evening service, and he took for his text the words, "And ye were its a firebrand plucked out of the burning." There was a large attendance at each service. Miss K. Hall ably discharged the duties of organist throughout the day. St. Luke's Church. Success attended the congregational tea party in con- nection with the above church which was held on Mon- day evening in the schoolroom, Liverpool-road. About 300 parishioners and friends sat down to tea. At the after proceedings,the Rev. H. R. Wild, curate-in-Charge, presided, and observed that the affairs of the parish had , gone on satisfqctorily during the past twelve months. ,1 The sale of work realized about £B5, and the money had beGn spent in necessary improvements and repairs to the church, &c. A small balance had been left in hand and it was being kept as a reserve fund. The entertainment was then proceeded with and was much enjoyed and appreciated. It was opened with an instrumental duet entitled "Eileen Alannah," given in good style by the ' Misses Burtham. •jThe other items on the programme were songs, recitations, and vocal quartettes by the Misses Longdin, Warren, Beesey and Pooley, and Messrs. H. G. Moseley and Jenks, and several members of the Apollo Male Voice aoir. Several were accorded an encore. Mr. Randall was an efficient accompanist. The concert was brought to a conclusion by a well-played humorous sketch entitled "Cross Purposes," and before the audience separated the Chairman thanked those who had given trays, those who had presided at the tea tables, and the artistes for their services.

div.head: Cairo-street Chapel. Annual Sermons and Congregational Tea Party.
div.p: Cairo-street Chapel. Annual Sermons and Congregational Tea Party.

The Rev. C. J. Street, M.A., L.L.8., of Bolton, preached the annual sermons at this place of worship, on Sunday, when there were goted congregations. On Monday evening the annual congregational tea party was held,and passed off very successfully. An excellent repast was partaken of by about two hundred members of the congregation and friends, lady members of the congregation preparing the tea and presiding at the tables. The room presented a bright and cheerful appearance, the pretty decorations for the Christmas party still remaining. After tea a meeting was held, the chair being occupied by Mr. F. Monks. Amongst others present were the Rev. E. W. Lummis, pastor; the Rev E. S. Hicks (Bolton), Mr. W. Long, Mr. C.Madeley, Mr. J. S. Hill. Mr. .1. A. Ewart, Mr. John Young, Mr. J. H. Knowles, and Mr. J. W. Davies, the last-named gentle- man efficiently discharging the secretarial duties. • The CHAIRMAN, in his very brief opening iemarks, wished success to Cairo-street Chapel and all its institu- tions. He was glad to see they still maintained a considerable number of young men of promise, and he thought that would always be the case. The Rev. E. W. Luatmts in speaking of the attend- ance at church said their small chapel was often pretty well filled, but he would like to see it filled to the splitting point so that they might feel they were a great success, and that they must see about building a new meeting house, or, perhaps enlarging the present one. He had been led recently to inquire why it was Unitarians—non-subscribing churchmen—as a whole had to be content with such meagre congregations in com- parison with other denominations. He fancied that only a small proportion of those who were lax church- goers were lax in their attention to their place—of busi- ness. He believed that most of them attended to their duty when they clearly perceived what it was, and they I made an effort to do it, and not a very great effort, he I imagined, was involved to set out on Sunday morning or evening to go to a place of worship. If they con- ceived it to be their duty to go to chapel they should certainly go. They did not consider it a great act of merit in itself. They would much rather see a man I leading an upright life, a loving life, with high aspire- tions, but lax in attendance at divine worship, than see I a mar/ regularly in his place on Sunday, but somewhat ' undistinguished by those virtues. To be a good man was much better than to be a regular chapel goer. In conclusion he thanked Mr. Hill, Mr. Hollingsworth, Mr. Pemberton, Miss Houghton and those who had helped him so devotedly in the Sunday school; Mr. Muir and the choir for their help in the Sunday service, and others, too numerous to mention, who had helped the work at Cairo-street so admirably during the year in all their varied and useful institutions. (Applause.) Mr.Hit.a. spoke of the work of the Sunday School which he said was in a flourishing condition. The work had been well carried on during the year; the numbers had been maintained, and there was every cause for congratulation. He was proud of the large number of scholars over sixteen years of age. Speaking of the necessity for more teachers Mr. Hill said Cairo-street Chapel had never lacked good men and women ft, main- tain the traditions of the place and it devolved upon the present members of the congregation to see that the work was carried on as efficiently as it had been in the past. The CHAIRMAN made some interesting observations with regard to the history of Cairo-street Chapel. He said there was no documentary evidence to be found in reference to it earlier than 1672. In all probability, when the Rector of Warrington was ejected from the Parish Church a considerable number of his parishioners went with him and formed themselves into a congre- gation which worshipped in the old court house that I used toistand in the Market-place. Mr. Long, would, perhaps, remember the old court house as well as he (Mr. Monks) did. In 1672 they got a licence to wor- ship in that building which, he believed, was their own, but he did not find a record of any chapel being built until Mr. Owen was the minister in the early part of' the eighteenth century. The first record he could find was 1715, when there was a small chapel, and in 1745 the old chapel was pulled down and some premises added to the freehold and the present chapel was built. In those days he believed that those who could not contribute money contributed labour in order that the chapel might be built. There was every probability that thei, , congregation was formed in 1662 and that they got th icence which hung in the vestry in 1672. How tha, licence was lost for so long to the congregation he did not know. It was in the possession of a gentleman in London, and it was by the merest accident they got to hear he had it. The gentleman came to 'Warrington and offered it to Mr. Nield, the then Mayor of Warrington, for £lO. Mr. Nield toldhim it did not concern him and that he would not buy it. It was taken away again, and he (Mr. Monks) happened to mention the fact to Mr. Paul Rylands, and told him that if ever he met the gentleman he had better buy the licence. Mr. Rylands said he knew the gentleman and that they could have the licence for £lO. That was how it came into the possession of the congregation. It had been defaced, there was the signature of King Charles the Second upon it, with the name of his minister. It was a genuine document and the original one. (Applause). The Rev. E. S. HICKS addressed the gathering and urged his hearers to greater efforts to promote the prosperity of the church. Mr. LONG, in proposing a hearty vote of thanks to all who had rendered assistance, congratulated the Cairo- street congregation upon the way in which it renewed its youth. He had been connected with the Chapel for a long time and could remember the days when Philip Carpenter was their Minister. He missed many faces that night—one in particular being their old friend Mr. Birchall—(applause)---without whom no Cairo-street meeting seemed complete. They all hoped that his in- disposition was a temporary one, and that he was only taking that care which a man of his years ought to do in the pr esent very changeable weather. They also missed from the younger section, Mr. and Mrs. F. W. Monks, whose enforced absence from home prevented them from beflig present. Mr. Long referred in appreciative terms to the services of all who had rendered assistance. Mr. KNOWLES seconded, and the motion was passed with acclamation,' the CHAIRMAN briefly responding. During the evening Miss Edith Birchall very sweetly sang " Baby seed song" and "Spring again," and Mr. Whitehouse was heard to advantage in "The sailor's grave " and "Oh promise me." Mr. J. M. Muir and Miss Birchall were the accompanists.

Latchford Baptist Improvement Society. ! At the weekly meeting of the above society on Monday evening n paper was read on "The Educa- tion Bill rate. should Nonconformists refuse to pay ?" by Mr. J. Pierce Williams. Mr. Williams said that the Nonconformists should abide by the law, and. Iwhen the opportunity came either by general election or otherwise, revoke the Act recently passed by Par- liament in a legitimate manner. Ile did not favour Ipassive resistance, and pointed out ma concise reason- able way why he stood by lawful channels. Several ! speakers supported the views embodied in the essay. I —The Rev. J. D. Matthews voiced the opposition, and ! said he could not conscientiously pay the rate in contradiction to his feelings on the matter, one section desiring arbitrary policy and lawful legitimate ; measures, and the other being inclined to favour • passive resistance.

Mn. RICHARD BELL, LABOUR AND THE who won from Mn. LEGISLATURE. GEOFFREY DRAGE the

seat formerly held at Derby by SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT, has been de- fending himself before a special meeting of repre- sentatives of Labour organisations. The charges brought against him are, we should say, curious and amusing rather than serious. He is accused of ,having been a "latter-day hack and bottle- holder of the official Liberal party." He is also alleged to have committed the offence of " figuring prominently at dinner-parties of Liberal stal- warts." The same charge is repeated in various forms, all of them abusive and unpleasant. Mr. Bell is said to have fallen under the influence of the Liberal Whips, to have "committed acts of treason to the workers," and have allowed his name to be adver- tised as chairman of the Liberal meeting in London. The member for Derby had little diffi- culty in repelling attacks of this kind. He showed that he has supported men of all views who have been helpful to, or are in future likely to help, the working classes. His aim in and out of Parliai ment,he says, is to support the interests of labour and in all his actions he has kept that object in view. A vote of confidence followed on these explanations, and Mr. BELL is safe for the present. Untilhe again dines with a " Liberal stalwart " even his calumniators may give him a rest.

_ Ridiculous as was the attack on Mr. BELL, and futile as it has proved, it possesses a more than ordinary importance in connection with the some- what extensive adoption of Labour candiiates that is being reported from some of the larger constituencies. These candidates, shoulti they be returned, are to form a separate group in the House of Commons. They are not to vote with either party as party men. They will be sent to Westminster as representatives of Labour simply and solely, and, as Mr. BELL'S case proves, they will have to be exceedingly careful as to those with whom they identify themselves either for prandial or political purposes. It is clear that without bringing themselves into critical relations with their supporters they will not be able to place their feet under any Liberal mahogany,either on a platform or at a dinner-party. Class representa- tion is an evil thing, but it exists. The landown- ing, the shipping, the railway, the mining, and the legal interests are all heavily represented in both Houses of Parliament, and when occasion arises each of these iLterssts, without hesitation, throws all its influence on its own side and in its own behalf. It is not at all surprising that labour should endeavour to improve on the example set by capital. Royal decisions in the Law Courts have even made it imperative that men should be

,ent to the House of Commons—whether spa cifi- cally as Labour representatives or not—who will make it their object to restore to the working classes the rights of which they have recently been deprived by the Law Courts. Acting together, of course, the working classes can make Par- liament what they like, and they can make it do as they like. But they do not act together. Some of them prefer Primrose League teas to the 'privilege of being represented by a member who woul4 oppose the taxation of their sugar and their bread. The bulk of them, so far,have preferred to 1111Pncrt candidates who come before them on political grounds. Even the Labour members in the House, with one or two exceptions, are politicians first. Has the condition of national feeling been so changed of late as to make it 'pro- bable that the working•class elector will hence- forth act as he has never acted hitherto? Has he .changedihis motives and renounced his convictions? Has he ceased to he Tory or Liberal, and become 'a purely class politician? If these questions can- not be answered in the affirmative it .is possible 'that the new method of putting forward Labour candidates may prove to be a disastrous blow to the interests of labour. It must be clear to those who consider the sub- ject even for a few moments that the object of 'bringing forward a candidateforParliament should be to secure his return. It must be a waste alike of force and of funds te bring )ca,..rd candidates 'who are obviously not to the taste of .any large 'body of electors. To bring forward candidates in .?Pen defiance of die bulk of those whose support is necessary for their return is, surely, gratuitous folly. Yet this is what is being done in some cases ancl without any such reasons as might be suppos- 'ad to exist. In the Liberal party there is no 'Prejudice against Labour representatives. They are always welcomed to the House of Commons. In some cages where they have exhibited special ability they have even been promoted to office. In 1892 there might have been a much increased instead of a much diminished Labour representation had certain leaders, or alleged leaders, of the Labour party accepted the co-operation that was offered. The Liberal Party is prepared at the next c:,rerieral election to adopt and to work with a laree number of -genuine 'representatives of labour. tinder these circum- stances it is worth while for the labour oNanisa- tions to ask whose interests are likely to be served by a pclicy of separate action. If candidates are nut forward with the declaration that they will have nothing to do with political parties, and Particularly with Liberalism, we,know at once who are the prime movers in the organisations by 'which they are supported. They are not 'To, perhaps; but they are certainly anti- Liberal. On what grounds can they ex- 'Peet Liberal candidates to statid aside in 'What they allege to be Labour interests, but that are not necessarily so? Labour and Liberalism Must be united, not thus defiant, if headway is to Ile made against the men at present in power. Nothing can save the Balfour Government at the next General Election but such 'tactics as those Which, for instance, drove JOHN MORLEY, one of the most earnest and most useful friends of Labour from the representation of Newcastle. The great- est interest of the worki:g man at this moment is it° get rid of the Government which has taxed his ha dr; Placed 'the education of his children in the the priests, burdened him with debt, and curtailed tive hialiberties. Should another Conserva- Go vernment be returned to power there will be another period of determined reaction. To Prevent this, Liberalism and Labour must come to such terms that where any candidate is put 'forward there will be at least a likelihood that he Will be returned to Parliament.

Once more the cigarette is the subject of marked .attention in the Press. A London halfpenny Paper has discovered that the chief evil of the Ilree is the fondness of the modern juvenile for ,the cheap and nasty cigarette. Brandy-balls, it is .suggested, have no longer any attraction for the 4or stolenschoolboy. _ Whether he has outgrown his taste apples may be a matter of ultimate dnoubt,but for these no outlay of pocket-money is uresearY. Every coin, according to our authority, ir;nether of public schoolboy or vendor of evening ir,Blsapar, goes to the tobacco shop for the do übt- toliry of five-a-penny whiffs. From this, of janTs,e, the most fearful effecte result. The penny 50,:„ are, purchased at the tuck-shop round the •&.,—.e,r, not only proven a toothsome morsel to hi'l4a minor, but in some small degree afforded st'T nourishment, and added to his girth and t,a,",nre• The cigarette, on the other hand, is i posi- t—e,Y deleterious, stunting the growth, and giving n 7 the features in childhood itself the wizened look Igte• Far be it from us to declare that there is no `ll‘a in the picture, though it seems to us, it ret .be confessed, very much overdrawn. In Merles. thirty-three States prohibit absolutely ;the. Vs of tobacco in any form to children; while in or tv - aY a bill is under consideration which will actually give to the police the power of taking out 2! their hands any capes or tobacco of which they "e 37 may be in possession. If, however, every Penny of pocket money is spent on the noxious 7,eed, what remains for the purchase of trashy 2wrature, the stories of boy scouts, and boy de- tectives, and boy highwaymen, which, as we know, t'renlate by hundreds and thousands, and more -urgently demand regulation, perhaps, than child- hood's use of the " fag ? div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
TIIE NEW ACT AT WIDNES.

Mary Cavan-a/c, of Caroline-street, was on Thursday charged at the Widnes Police Court with being drunk, and with having with her at the time a child under seven. 'Fhe case having been proved a fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed, or in default seven days. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS. Mr. R. H. Posnett, J.P., of Runcorn, was one of the speakers at a Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Convention held in the Brunswick Chapel, Moss-street, Liverpool, on Monday. In the course of his remarks ha pleaded for personal service and pointed out that in Hyderabad, in which his brother and sister were working among twelve millions of people there were only thirty mis- sionaries.

div.head: CHARITY CONCERT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CHARITY CONCERT AT RUNCORN.

On Monday evening a successful concert in aid of James Harrison, 4, Wivern-place, Runcorn, who eleven years ago met' with an accident which rendered him in- capable of earning his livelihood, was given by Mr. H. Berrey's Operatic Company in the Public Hall. Mr. S. Taylor presided. A high-class entertainment of a most acceptable character WftB given by the company, the members of which included Mrs. Tabernacle, the Misses Berrey, Parr, Griffiths, Dennett, Greenhalgh and Richard and Messrs. Gleave, Hamblett, Milne, Atherton, Cotton and Rigby. The financial result of the concert was satisfactory. THEFT OF A LAMP AT WESTON,

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. A Thomas and other magistrates, Charles Whit- march, of Weston, was charged with having stolen a paraffin oil lamp, the property of James Rowbottom, of Weston, on Saturday night. From the evidence it appeared that defendant was at the house in the early evening, and left at the same time that prosecutor's daughter went out. Prosecutor went to sleep on the sofa, and while he slumbered defendant re-entered the house and took away the lamp which stood lighted on the table. He broke it when he got away and threw the pieces in different directions. A little girl had, however seen him in the house, and information having been given to P.C. Wylie he saw the defendant and accused him of the theft. He replied that he knew nothing about it. Defendant now pleaded guilty. He said he was drunk and did not know what he was doing. He was fined 10s.

div.head: WESTON DROWNING MYSTERY,
div.p: A WESTON DROWNING MYSTERY,

Mr. Dobson, district coroner, conducted an inquiry at the Royal Oak Hotel, Weston, on Saturday afternoon into the circumstances attending the death of Peter Connelly, a labourer at Weston Bone Works, whose body was recovered from the river Weaver on the 6th inst. Mr. W. H. Williams was foreman of the jury.— Louisa Pritchard, 5, Peel-street,Runcorn, said she identi- fied the body as that of her uncle. He was 52 years of age. She last saw him alive on January 10th. He called at her house and asked her to assist him. He said he had been out of work for three weeks. She could not take him in, but she gavehim 4s. 6d. He said he would go to Frodsham to look for work and he would see her again if he was not successful. He was a single man withno one dependent upon him. He did not seem de- pressed. He was in his usual spirits and well in health, except that he was going blind in the left eye.—By Superintendent Ennion : He was a steady man, but not a teetotaller. She remembered calling at the Police Station a fortnight ago to inquire about a rumour that Connelly had been found deaden Frodsham Marsh.—By Mr. Haining : Deceased had been subject to fits in his earlier days but not lately to her knowledge.— John Helsby, minor, of Clifton, said he was walking between the Weaver Canal and the river about one o'clock on the 6th of February when close to Weston Works he saw the body of the deceased floating in an upright position in the river Weaver. He recovered the body with assistance and sent for the police.—P.C. Wylie said he had theabody conveyed to the Royal Oak Hotel. There was a slight bruise on the forehead, both eyes and the bridge of the nose were discoloured, and there was discolouration on each side of the throat. In the pockets of the clothing were • Is. llid. in money, a pocket knife and some tobacco. He should say the body had been in the canal at least three weeks. He could not say whether the marks were done before or after death. A verdict of "Found dead "was returned.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD- OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD- OF GUARDIANS.

• The fortnightly meeting of the above authority was held on Tuesday at the Frodstuun Petty Sessional Court House. Present :—Messrs. J. Stokes (in the chair), A. R. Norman (vice-chairman), S. Taylor, T. Woods, J. Douglas; the members of the Rural District Council, with Messrs. G. F. Ashton (clerk),W. E. Hongh (assist- ant clerk), T. Cook, J. Riley, T. DePrez (relieving o ilicers).

div.head: WAR OFFICE PAYMENTS.
div.p: WAR OFFICE PAYMENTS.

A letter was received from the Chief Paymaster of the Home District stating that the Secretary of War had considered the Board's request for the pument to Thomas Burgess other than quarterly in advance and had consented to the payment being made monthly in advance. _ _ _
The Clerk said the letter was one sent in reply asking that the man Burgess be paid weeky instead of quarterly
ANNUAL -rood LAW CONFERENCE.

The Clerk reported that the annual meeting of the Central Poor Law Conference would be held at the London Guildhall on Monday 10th and 11th. The sub- jects to be discussed are "Labour Colonies in Relation to the Poor Law." "What is adequate relief ?" and the treatment of the feeble-minded Delegates from the Board were invited to attend. _
Mr. Wright proposed that delegates be sent as usual to the Council and that he would propose the names at the next meeting.
THE ST-ATE OF THE WORKHOUSE

_ A letter was read from Dr. Selby, dated February 10th, stating that he had visited the Workhouse at 10.30 that day and was pleased to report there were no fresh cases of small-pox. Quarantine would be up on Thurs- day noon the 12th February. He quite approved of the recommendations of the Master to put the house in order. The hospital wards had required doing through- out for some time. The Chairman : The suspicious case reported at the Board's last meeting has proved to be not a small-pox case?
The Clerk : Yes. THE MASTER'S REPORT.

The Clerk read a report from the Master of the Work- house, Mr. Cunnah, stating that he had thoroughly dis- infected the oakum picked up by suspected contacts. He recommended that the rooms and possages fre- quented by the Guardians be painted and disinfected. He would prepare specifications for the tenders. On the motion of Mr. Mosely-Williams, seconded by Mr. Linaker it was resolved that a small committee with the Clerk be appointed to accept tenders. Mr. Woods asked whether the relieving officers could not notify the master of anysuspicious cases that might come from any lodging house. Mr. Linaker thought that the Workhouse officials and the medical officer would take all the precautions necessary. -
The Clerk pointed ont that the master kept a record of all vagrants and persons using the Workhouse.
A. DEBIT BALANCE. The financial statement presented by Mr. Woodward showed that there was an adverse balance against the Board of £2329 10s. 2d.

div.head: Examiner, Friday, February 13, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Friday, February 13, 1903.
LICENSING SESSIONS. RUNCORN. Petition For a Reduction of Licences.

The first licensing sessions under the new Act were held at the Runcorn Sessions House on Monday. The justices present were Messrs. A. Thomas (in the chair), S. Taylor, A. R. Norman, E. Imison, James Pritchard, G. L. Davies and J. Ockleston. There was a large at- tendance of the public.

div.head: POLICE REPORT.
div.p: THE POLICE REPORT.

Superintendent Ennion, in his report for the year ending December 31st last, stated that there were 44 licensed victuallers, 52 beersellers, and five others who sold off the premises—s total of 101. This gave an average of 206 of population to each licence. No licenced victuallers had been proceeded against during the year. In the previous year one was proceeded against but not convicted. One beerseller had been proceeded against but not convicted. In the previous yearithree were proceeded against and one was convicted. A hundred and forty persons were proceeded against for drunkenness during the year. Of this number 135 were convicted. In the preceding year 175 were proceeded against and 165 were convicted; No licensed victualler or beerseller had been convicted since the Brewster Sessions in August, 1901 (16 months). There was a decrease of 34 persons proceeded against and 30 persons convicted for drunkenness as compared with the previous year. He was directed by the Chief Constable to draw the magistrates' attention to the back entrance to the Mill Stone Inn, Mill-street, Runcorn, kept by Thomas Leyland. The back entrance to the premises opened into a..yard common to five cottages and proper police supervision was thereby frustrated. He had also to draw attention to the Red Lion Inn, Halton, kept by Thomas Parker. The sanitary arrangements at that house were very unsatisfactory and quite unfit for I licensed premises.
THE TEMPERANCE LEAGUE PETITION FOR A REDUCTION.

Mr. Harry Baker, chemist, Moughland-lane, Runcorn, presented a petition on behalf of a deputation from the Runcorn Temperance League. The other Members of the deputation were the Revs. W. A. Eyre and T. S. Morris and Messrs. T. Wood, J. Reynolds W. Shaw, W. Handley, S. Littler Captain Taylor (Salvation Army), and T. Leech (secretary). The Revs. A. Wells, W. T. Coppin, J. B. Forster and J.-Osborne were unable to at- tend, The Rev. Canon Wood. wrote: In common with many people wiser than myself I urge the diminution of the number of licences, mainly for the public good, but without any "arriere pensee" of making ultimately illegal to buy or sell intoxicants altogether. The petition was as follows:—" To the licensing justices assembled at the general annual licensing meeting. Gentlemen,—We, the deputation organized by the Runcorn Temperance League thank you for granting the permission to come before you. We are fully convinced that the number of houses in Runcorn licensed for the sale of intoxicating liquors. namely 87, is greatly in excess of the requirements 9f the population, being one licence for every 33 families, and therefore humbly pray your worships to take into your very careful consideration the desirability of re- ducing them for the better government of the town,and we have the more hope as other licensing justices in various parts of the country have already made marked reductions and as you have recently had increased powers given you in the new Licensing Act for the better control of the traffic in intoxicating liquors. Though your present petitioners are only few in num- leer they, nevertheless, represent the prayer of 1,100
The Chairman: We are very much obliged to you or this petition, and it shall have our consideration.
APPLICATION FOR AN OFF BEER LICENCE.

For the eight time Mr. G. Partington applied, through Mr. Madden, barrister, Liverpool, for an off beer licence. Mr. Lake appeared for the Temperance League. The case was argued at great length at the conclusion (of which the bench said that there was no change from the circumstances of last year and the application could not be granted.

div.head: RENEWAL OF LICENCES,
div.p: RENEWAL OF LICENCES,
The Magistrates' Clerk called the list of licensees,and the whole of the licences were renewed.
THE RED LION AND MILLSTONE BEERHOUSES.

Mr. Lake, referring to the superintendent's remarks upon these houses, said he was instructed by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., to state that lithe defects at the Red Lion were in way of being remedied. They had purchased the cottages adjoining, and they would be pulled down. Plans for the alteration would be sub- mitted as soon as they were made out. He understood the proposed alterations were satisfactory to the Superintendent. The same remarks applied to the Mill- stone Inn. Steps were being taken to meet t 11(. objection. THE SAILORS' HOME. • REQUEST FOR CHANGE OF SAME.

When the name of the Sailors' Home public-house was called, Mr. W. Shaw, missioner for the local branch of the Mersey Mission to Seamen, asked the magistrates whether it was possible to have the name of the house changed. In nearly all seafaring towns in England, he I said, the Sailor's Home was an institution to which sailors, especially steady men, went to be away from 1 the temptation of drink. When they entered a town they asked for the Sailors' Home, and the name of this house was very misleading. The Rev. W. A. Eyre supported what Mr. Shaw had said. It was misleading to have a public-house called the Sailor's Home. As Mr. Shaw had said the Sailors' Home in seafaring towns was a place in which the men went to be away from drink. His own son, who was a ship's officer, was very much surprised when he observed the name of this house. If a reCommendation went from the magistrates it would be more likely to brill,*' about the desired result than if Mr. Shaw made the application. Mr. Butterworth (on behalf of Messrs. Givenall, Whitley and Co.) suggested that Mr. Shaw shonld write to the firm.
BAGATELLE LICENCES.
Three applications for bagatelle licences were granted

div.head: NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS. • -HEAVY INCREASE IN DRUNKENNESS.
div.p: NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS. • -HEAVY INCREASE IN DRUNKENNESS.
FULL LICENCE FOR A CROFT INN AGAIN REFUSED.
At Nea-ton-le-Willows Police Court on Thursday the annual Brewster Sessions for the Warrington Petty SeAsional Division were held. Mr. T. J. Gillespie presided over a full bench of magistrates.

div.head: POLICE REPORTS.
div.p: THE POLICE REPORTS.

HEAVY INCREASE IN DRUNKENNESS. Superintendent Cocker presented the annual report for the Warrington district which- includes Newton, Earlestown, Croft, Winwick, &c. He stated that there was a total of sixty-seven licences. During the past two years the licences of thirteen licensed victuallers and four beersellers had been transferred. During the past two years only two licensed persons were proceeded against, one being dismissed and the other ordered to pay costs. The number of people summoned for drunkenness during 1901 was 121 (including fourteen females) and 189 (including thirteen females) in 1902, while in 1901 156 persons had been apprehended, and 185 in 1902, making a total of 277 persons charged with drunkenness in 1901 and 373 in 1902, an increase of 97. There were three applications for hearing—viz., Isaac Mains, beerseller, Horseshoe Inn, Croft, to sell all intoxicating liquors for consumption on or off the premises ; Edward Leigh Bent, beerseller, Vulcan Inn, Newton, billiard licence ; John Pearson, refreshment, house-keeper, 8, Oxford-street, Earlestown, billiard licence.

Superintendent Cocker, after reading his report, said he took objection to the renewal Of the licence of the Limerick Inn, Bitrtonwood, and asked for that to stand over until the adjourned licensing sessions. Superintendent O'Mara, (if the Wigan district, pre- sented his report, which showed that within the town- ships of Haydock and Golborne which form the Wigan portion of the Warrington Petty Sessional- Division, there , were 33 licensed persons. 13 innkeepers, 1 spirit grocer, 1 licensed to sell wine (off), and 18 beersellem (13 on and 5 off the premises), being an increase of 1 as compared with the year 1901. The number of persons proceeded against for drunkenness was 179, an increase of 34. There were no applications for the magistrates' consideration.

The Chairman said he was exceedingly sorry to see such a very heavy increase of drunkenness daring the year. The licences would be renewed except that of the Limerick beerhouse, Burtonwood, which was adjourned. Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, on behalf of the Earles- town Licensed Victuallers' Association, said that the association intended to carry out the new Act with the same loyalty and discretion as they had done the other Acts.
THE APPLICATIONS.
FULL LICENCE FOR A CROFT INN REFUSED.

Mr. H. J. Longton made application on behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. for alterations to the Butcher's Arms, Sankey. The alterations were sanctioned. An application for alterations to the bedroom accom- modation of the Viaduct Hotel,Earlestown,was granted. The billiard licence for the Vulcan Inn was granted, subject to an undertaking being given to Superintendent Cocker to close the billiard-room at the same time as the licensed house,. Mr. Longton, on behalf of Mr. H. L. Riley, of St. Helens applied for a billiard licence for John Pearson, refreshment housekeeper, 8, Oxford-street, Ilarlestown. This was granted. The application of Isaac Maines, beerseller, for a full licence for the Horseshoe Inn, Croft, was next dealt with. Maines, in his evidence, said that the rate- payers of the district had signed the petition for a full licence, and everybody was wishful for it, even the county coroner. In reply to Superintendent Cocker, Maines said that the population was 970, and there were five licensed houses in the district, which worked out at one house for 194 persons. • Several witnesses gave evidence in support of the ap- plication. Mr. Hatton -.stated that in ten years there had only been an increase in the population of twenty-two, and there was no alteration of circqmstances between the time of the two applications, which were refused, and
the present time. The bench retired for a few minutes, and on returning the chairman said the magistrates unanimously declined to grant the licence.

div.head: DARESBURY.
div.p: DARESBURY.
THE BACK ENTRANCE OF THE MULBERRY TREE INN.

Mr. William Long presided at the annual licensing ' Sessions for the Daresbury Division, held on Tuesday morning in the Court House, Daresbury. There were ' also present on the Bench Roger Parr, Colonel Ridgway, •Mr. H. Nield and Mr. Joseph Knowles. Superintendent Ennion presented his annual report, on the conduct of licensed victuallers and beer retailers, in the division. He stated that there were 23 licensed victuallers, one beer seller, and two off-licence holders in the division, making a total of 26 licences. No licensed victuallers or beersellers had been proceeded against during the year, being a decrease of one pro- ceeded against and none convicted in the preceding year. Twenty-six persons had been proceeded against for drunkenness, all of whom were convicted, as com- pared with 21 persons proceeded against, and all con- victed during the preceding year. No licensed victuallers or beersellers had been convicted since the Brewster Sessions held in August, 1901. There was an increase of five persons proceeded against, and five per- sons convicted for drunkenness compared with the pre- ceding year. He had been directed by the Chief Constable to draw attention to the back entrance of the Mulberry Tree Inn, Stockton Heath, kept by Priscilla Newall. The back entrance to this house opened into a yard common to six cottages, and proper police super- vision was thereby frustrated. _ _

The Chairman said the magistrates were very pleased to hear so favourable a report, and they could only hope that matters would go on still further improving. In the administration of the new Act he thought that by moderation shown by the Bench—which he hopedwould always be the case—still further improvements might be brought about, especially by the working together of the licensed victuallers and the Bench in every way that could promote temperance. Superintendent Ennion remarked that he had seen the landlady, who had promised to carry out certain im- provements before next Brewster Sessions. The Clerk: We had better adjourn that until the next transfer day.

The Chairman: All the licences will be renewed with the exception of the Mulberry Tree Inn, which will be adjourned in order to see what arrangements can be made for the improvements suggested by the Chief Constable.

Mr. Browne, solicitor, suggested that it would be interesting to have in future reports the percentages— of the number of people to every licence, Ste. He was sure this division would show a great advantage over other divisions and towns.

The Chairman observed that this division occupied a very good position, and he would be glad to have Mr. Browne's suggestion ratified. The Superintendent said he would see what could be done in the matter.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DiSFRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DiSFRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of the above Council was held on Tuesday, Mr. J. Knowles presiding. Present Messrs. T. Wright, J. Stokes, C. E. Linaker, A. Greenwa,y, A. H. Talbot, E. Clarke, T. Darlington, J. M. Williams, T. Lewis, S. Woodward, W. Ellison, S Horton, P. Gleave, J. Nickson, J. N. Bagguley, A. Dean, R. Pilling, A. Wallington, J. B. Chadwick, A. G. Guest, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), J. Swinton (surveyor), J. Farrington (inspector).

div.head: MANCHESTER PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY'.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY'.

A circular was produced drawing attention to an inquiry to be held at the Town Hall, Manchester, on Wednesday,FebruarylBth, with regard to the representa- tion of the Ellesmere Port and Whitby Urban District Council upon the Port Sanitary Authority. It was resolved that the Clerk and Mr.,). M. Williams attend the inquiry.—Mr. Williams, who is a member of the Port Sanitary Authority, pointed out that the in- clusion of the two authorities would not make any financial differencs as Chester was being relieved of some of its financial responsibilities.

THE RUNCORN WATER. The Clerk reported receipt of a letter from the Runcorn Urban Council to the effect that the Rural District Council's letter re the Halton and Weston water supply had been referred to the Water Committee. The Clerk: It does not go very far. But if I don't hear from them shortly I will write again.

A BAD ROAD. Mr. Ainsworth wrote pointing out that the road in Marsh fields was not fit to walk upon. The Clerk said he would forward a copy of the letter to the Surveyor, who would report at the next meeting.

THE UNEMPLOYED PROBLEM. Mr. Percy Alden, hon. secretary of the National Unemployed Comm ittee,fo rwarded a circular announcing a National Conference of public authorities and work- ing men's organizations to be hgd in the Guild Hall, London, on February 27th, and inviting the Board to send representatives. The conference was the outcome of the distress due to lack of employment. The Clerk said the circular affected the London poor more than anybody else. It was resolved that the letter lie on the table. THE EDUCATION Am'. -

The President of the Yorkshire Rural District Clerk's Association, Mr. H. Reaumont, wrote with reference to the Education Act, that at a meeting of the Association held atjWakefield, the provisions of the new Act were discussed, and it. was decided that Clerks to Guardians should be urged to approach the County Council in which the Union is situate, inviting them to appoint an Education Committee for the area of each Union.
THE AUDITOR'S CERTIFIC ATE.
- The auditor's certificate was produced by the Clerk which showed that the books were properly kept.
TO. PROTECT THE COUNC

A letter was read from the Association of District Councils with reference to the North Western Power Gas Bill recommending the Council to join the Associa- tion in supporting the Bill,provided each Council could get protective clauses. In order to further this end the representatives of each Council were asked to contribute a sum of £5 ss. On the motion of Mr. Linaker it was resolved that the Council vote the sum of .E 5 ss. in order to secure necessary protective clauses. THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT,
Dr. Adams reported that there were no fresh out- breaks of small-pox. The hospital water was satis- factory and the new sewage saleine would be com- pleted in a few days. A DANGER OF INFECTION?

_ Mr. Wallington asked whether there was any danger likely to be caused by the sheets that vere used at the Sanatorium being sent to Frodsham to be washed. Mr. Linaker : We cannot stop them being sent any- where. _
Mr. Wallington: Ts it injurious to the public health?
Mr. ',looker : People will he afraid to live just now.
Mr. Stokes: Are they sent to a public wash house. A Member. There is no public wash house in Frodsham.
_ Mr. Wright: They are sent to a wash house just above Overton. _ _ _

Mr. Wallington said the hedges on the high way were used for drying purposes. He thought there was a possibility of infection. Mr. Woodward ridiculed the idea that those very people—scientists of the Liverpool Sanatorium—should take the means to spread about the very disease they were trying to stamp out. The suggestion was ridicu- lous on the face of it.
Mr. Wallington: I want the Medical Meer to give his opinion. Is there any risk? The Medical Officer : 1 should say there is no risk whatever.

div.head: BRUNSWICK-ROAD, MISSION HALL.
div.p: BRUNSWICK-ROAD, MISSION HALL.

A concert in connection with the above was held in the Mission Room, Brunswick-road, on Saturday even- ing. The programme was given by the members of the Earlestown Wesleyan Choir and the Brunswick Male Quartet. The outstanding feature of a capital pro- gramme was a duet given by Misses Minnie Barr and Alice Jackson entitled "O'er the hawthorn hedge "a splendid rendering eliciting Nell merited applause. Other items were : Quartet "In absence" the Bruns- wick Male Quartet ; song, "Another day" Miss Miriam Jackson; song, "The anchor'g weighed" Mr. J. Eckers- ley ; recitation, Mrs. Francis ; song, "Love the pedlar" Miss Minnie Barr ; quartet " Simple Simon " Male Quartet ; song, " Asthore " Miss Alice Jackson ; song, "Alice where art thou "Mr. .1. Eckersley ; song, "When the heart is young" Miss Miriam Jackson; recita- tion, Mrs Francis; song, "The King's Own" Mr. Mather; quartet, " A catastrophe " Male Quartet. Mrs. Goslin was the accompanist.

THE STRONGEST MAN ON EARTH.

This was the subject of a lecture given on Monday evening-by the Rev. Aked of Liverpool in the Con- gregational schoolroom Newton, on behalf of the Newton Mutual Improvement Society. The Rev. James Allott presided and there was a large audience. The lecturer took as his standard Heinrich Ibsen, and mentioned the several plays he had written. Ibsen ranked very high amongst the intellectual forces of our modern world. We were told that his playa were obscene rubbish, that he was an insane old fraud, anda dirty old humbug. It was easy to say those and hundreds of other thinks about any great man who had not passed the criticism of his mortals. Nobody who had ever felt the Ibsen grip upon his soul should wonder that he spoke to them in- such thrilling terms as those. There was one great play of lbsen's called " Ghosts," before which terrible play man's imagination reeled. The strongest man on earth was the man who stood most alone. Amongst strong men he instanced Emerson, the prophet of New England; Martin Luther; Oliver Cromwell, the strongest 'man England had ever produced; John Wesley and Garibaldi. A vote of thanks to the lecturer closed the gathering. LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SHOES, UNDER the CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Advt. H. M. ~—..... should be given publicity, and, consequently, two or three rather interesting facts were revealed. Not only did Dr. Adams admit that the girl was suffering rather severely, but he also confessed that the girl was actu- ally bedded in the only living room. Dr. Adams' explanation that the girl was downstairs rather than upstairs because she would have monopolised the only sleeping room, will appear to all reasonable minds a singularly feeble one. To the ordinary lay mind it appears that the risks of infection, especially in the peeling state of the disease, would be far greater in a room where food was prepared, rather than isola- ted in a bedroom even though the • occupants had Meanwhile to put up with serious inconveni- , enee. Of course, it was impossible for the girl to be I removed to Dutton Workhouse, when there is no isola- • tion hospital as in Warrington, but, surely, had Dr. Adams w shed to isolate a case sufficiently grave to cause alarm to a populous district, Runcorn or Warring- ton could have been approached to render service to the community. The singular part of the business is that, according to Mr. Wallington, who evidently knew more about the case than the majority, Dr. Leadbetter is not lat. present attending the girl at all, who, meanwhile, has had a serious relapse. div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

MEASLES AND ECZEMA AT EARLESTOWN. Measles are rampant amongst the 'school children of Earlestown, and. there is talk of closing one of the schools. At St. Mary's Roman Catholic schools there are numerous cases of eczema, bat steps are being taken to stamp out this irritating complaint. ENFORCING THE NEW 'ACT.
At Newton Petty Sessions on. Thursday, Margaret Hill was tined 10s. and costs for being drunk in charge of a child under seven years of age. This was the first case of the kind in the division.

THE ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A GM. .AT GOLBORNE. At Warrington Occasional COurt on :Monday, Edward Forrester, of Gelborne, was committed for trial at the Liverpool Assizes on the charge of indecently assaulting Lilly Dutton aged seven years at GO'borne on January 30th.

div.head: THEFT IND ,ASSAULT.
div.p: THEFT IND ,ASSAULT.

David Mitwson, of Haydock,.l;;. -charged on remand at Nowton on Thursday, with stealing a quantity of tools belonging to John MS,- of Glasgow, from the extension works of the Smallpox Hospital at Haydock, The prisoner was further charged with assaulting Con- stable Thomas, who arrested* him. Alawson denied the charge, and said he had bought the tools.—He was fined 40s. and costs in each case, or two months' hard labour. . _niM SHEEP WORRYING. AT NEWTON.

At Newton, on Thursday, John Jones, of Earlestown, was sued for 20s. damages under the Dog Act, in respect of sheep-worrying, alleged to have been done by defend- ant's dog to sheep. of Messrs. Stone, Newton Park It was stated that defendant's dog got among the sheep and worried some of them. Mr. Knowles stated that publicity regarding the responsibilities of dog-owners permitting worrying was desirable, and defendant was fined 20s. and costs.

div.head: ST. PETER'S CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL.
div.p: ST. PETER'S CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The Annual Soiree in connection with the teaching staff of St. Peter's Church Sunday School was held in the Town Hall, Newton on Wednesday evening. The room was very prettily decorated, and about 50 couples were present. Music was supplied by Messrs Peplow and Walker, and dancing was indulged in from 8 o'clock until 2 o'clock nexttnoming.Refreshments were supplied by Mrs. Ring.

div.head: VESTRY MEETING AT 'NEWTON.
div.p: VESTRY MEETING AT 'NEWTON.

A meeting of ratepayers was called for Wednesday. evening at the Town Hall, Newton, for the purpose of approving a statement asked for by the County Council as the gross value of assessments in the district of Newton-in-Makerfield. The ratepayers took no interest in the matter, and beyond overseers and members of the& Press, there were none present. The gross value of the township in October 1897 was £80,378, with a net rate- able value of £67,568. At the present time the gross value is £86,389 10s., and the rateable value £71,818. The statement was approved.
NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL LOCAL ACTS.

On Wednesday afternoon, Mr. E. P. Baird held an in- quiry at the Town Hall, Earlestown, with reference to the application of the District Council for the amend- ment of certain local Acts conferring borrowing powers upon the Council, and to vary the security given or to be given for any stuns borrowed or to be borrowed for the purposes of the gas or water undertakings of the COuncil. The only members of the Council present were Dr. Latham and Mr. T. Ormand, none of the public being present. The report was read to the inspector by Mr. C. Cole, and the proceedings afterwards closed.

div.head: SMART CAPTURE AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: SMART CAPTURE AT EARLESTOWN.

A smart capture has been effected by Constable Lennie of Earlestown. He received information that a valuable overcoat had been taken from Mr. Austin's house in King-street, and seeing a man of the working class•type wearing it, he questioned him, and ultimately arrested him. His prisoner has turned out to be Daniel Jones, who has several aliases, of Llanberis. He has a long list of convictionsagainst hitn, including highway robbery with violence, for which he received fifteen lashes with the" cat," and four months' hard labour. Prisoner on Thursday was remanded until Tuesday next. Acc [DEVI' TO A FOOTB AL LER.

On Saturday during the progress of the match between Earlestownand Damen, Bartley of the home team and Haslam of Darwen collided violently, with the result that the latter sustained a fracture of the collar bone. He retired to the pavillion, and was attended to by Inspector Forster, who happened to be on the field and a couple of ambulance men, the injured bone beiag put iato position; and the man mAde coinfortstble to enable hint to return to•Darwea without fear of further injury.

div.head: P.S.A.
div.p: P.S.A.

Thensual weekly meeting of the Earlestown and Dis- trict P.S.A. was held in the CO-operative Hall, Earle- street, on Sunday afternoon. The hall was as usual' well filled. Mr. Maclin presided. An excellent address on "The Manliness of Jesus" was given by Mr. George Dring: Several vocal items were rendered by Miss• Bennison. Mrs. Francis contributed several' recita- tions, and Miss Potter was the hymn soloist. Miis Williamson presided at the piano and Mr. IL Smith at the organ.

Flannagan,.John Burke and T. Glynn.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES
A DISPUTED TENANCY.

Daresbury Petty Sessions. on Tuesday Samuel Lewis,'sen., and Samuel Lewis, jun., of Lower Whitley were charged with stealing 34 cwt of manure, the pro- perty of Edward Cannon, of Whitley, and of the value of 128.7 on the 6th January, Mr. Browne prosecuted.—Mr. Steel, who appeared for the defendants, pleaded not guilty,—Mr. Browne stated that owing to some juggling between father and son, Mr. Meadows, the agent for Sir George Chetwode, gave notice to the defendants to quit on the 31st July. The farm was taken on an agree- ment, by which they should vacate all stubble land on the Ist of November. The notice to do so was served, but they did not quit. On the 19th December Mr. Meadows gave the ingoing tenant (Mr. Cannon) possession of the land, and on the 6th of January he sent one or two loads of manure to be put on the stubble field. It was put on, but the defendants were seen by ex-P.C. Crowder to order it to be taken away. Ex-P.C. Crowder, who lived in a cottage overlooking the land, asked him why he was taking it away, The younger defendant said he was going to put it on Mr. Leach's farm, and he would sell or give away any more which was put on the land. He contended that Mr. Cannon was deprived by the defendants of the owner- ship and possession of the manure, and they were trying by trickery to defeat the agent and the ingoing tenant. Ex-P.C. Crowder then gave evidence in support of Mr. Browne's statement. In cross-examination by Mr. Steel witness said he did not consider, when he saw the manure being removed, that it was a felony. He thought the defendant was asserting his right as tenant of the farm. —Mr. Steel contended that it had not been proved that defendants had any felonious intention; and, further,he submitted that the jurisdiction of the Court was ousted. The elder defendant was still entitled to remain on the farm for a time, which question was in dispute. The object of the case was- undoubtedly to get possession of the land,but the elder defendant claimed to be the tenant until certain compensation was 'paid.—The de- fendants gave evidence, and said they refused to allow the manure to be put on the field until the tenancy dis- pute was settled. The prosecutor could have the manure from where it now was at any time.—Defendants were fined £1 and costs each.

div.head: Disorderly Tram Passenger.
div.p: A Disorderly Tram Passenger.

In consequence of his unseemly behaviour on a -tram car on Monday night, John Cragan, of Grappen- hall, made his appearance before Alderman Sutton and other magistrates at the Borough Police Court on .Tuesday, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Rylands-street—Michvel Flannery, a checker in the Tramways department, • said he hoarded the 8.50 car to Latchford in Knintsford-road. Prisoner, who was under the influence of drink, was inside the car, and was shouting and swearing. Witness cautioned him hut prisoner would not desist from his conduct and witness asked for his name and address. Prisoner refused to supply the information and went on the top of the car, where he continued his bad behaviour until the terminus was reached. He was again asked for his name and address but refused to give it and tried to force his way off the car. He was prevented from leaving and conveyed back to Bylauds-street. He re- fused to give his name and address to P.C. Andrews and was locked up—A fine of 10s. with the option of fourteen days imprisonment was imposed. .A Soldier's than Theft.

A mean theft came before the notice_ of the magis- trates at the Warrington Police Court on Monday, -when a young man named Harry Appleby was charged -with being an absentee from the North Staffordshire Regiment, stationed at Lichfield, and stealing Bs. from the house of James Birchall, 23, Plumptou-street, Warrington. The Chief Constable said the prisoner was arrested on Saturday by P.C. Hodgkiss for being an absentee. It afterwards transpired that he had com- mitted a theft from the house where he had been lodging. Mrs. Birchall stated that about three months ago prisoner enlisted, and his wife then went to lodge with her. They heard no more of him until Saturday, the 31st ult. when he went to Mrs. Birchall's and said he was having a short furlough. He remained until Wednesday, on which day Mrs. Birchall left her purse, containing Bs. which was all the money she possessed in the cupboard. When she went for it the following morning the money was gone, and prisoner on being questioned denied any knowledge of it. The matter remained a mystery until prisoner's arrest when it was found he had been spending money freely in •drink, and he admitted taking the money. He left Mrs. .Birchall penniless, the Bs. being the rent money. Prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment, after which term he will be handed over to the military authorities. P.C. Hodgkiss was recommended for the usual reward for the arrest.

div.head: AN ATMOSPHERE OF BANK NOTES. Bank of Engiancl Foils Forgers.
div.p: AN ATMOSPHERE OF BANK NOTES. Bank of Engiancl Foils Forgers.

The Bank of England's immunity from forged notes arises from the difficulty of imitating the famous paper on which they are printed. It is made near Overton, Hants, says the " Hants Observer," quoting the word of a man who as he remarked,"bad lived in an atmosphere of bank notes all his life." That atmosphere had not always proved beneficial to him. "Some time ago," said this man, a Mr. Leonard Roberts, Winchester- street, Overton, " I was, in consequence of getting wet, attacked with rheumatism in my left leg. I gradually grew worse, but, in spite of trying many remedies, I got no relief until I tried Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. Before I took the pills the pains in my legs were so excruciating that I frequently fell down in agony when I tried to move. I. had to give up my work as a carter on a farm, and at length went into the hospital at Winchester, where I stayed seven weeks. Afterwards I went to the seaside for a month. - -

"The hospital treatment did me no good, and the sea- side very little, but about six months ago I read about some remarkable cures by Dr. Williams' pink pills, and obtained a box of them. By the time I had used it I was able to get about pretty well. I continued taking the pills until I had used three boxes, by which time I not only felt stronger, but could walk without pain. I am now better than I have been for years, in fact I seem quite changed." Liniments and embrocations will not cure rheuma- tism ; neither will purgatives : you might as well. ex- pect so cure anaemia with them, or kidney disease. All these things Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people are constantly curing,as well as consumption,bronchitis, eczema,flts,gout,heart disease,paralysis,and the ailments which women sufferin silence. It is the genuine pills,no substitutes (which some shopmen push), that cure. The full name on the pink wrapper is a guarantee of genuiness. An instance of their special value to women at critical times will be found in another part of this paper. wew Dragonflies.

An interesting paper on " Dragonflies " was read before the members of the Warrington Field Club at the second meeting of the second winter session, by Mr.. Howarth. Of these bold and beautiful, though ferocious insects there are 39 species which occur in Britain. After briefly dealing with their classifica- tion, both amongst themselves, and in relation to other groups, and pointing out some of the characteristic features of the anatomy of larym and adults, the lec- turer proceeded to explain at greater length the pro- cesses of fertilization and deposition of the eggs and the life history of the larva, reserving a fuller treat- ment of the adult forms fr anotner paper. Mr Howarth exhibited a number ol beautifully preserved specimens—though in these, as. in many other cases, the colours fade quickly after death—and had pre- pared, sith the help of Mr. A. Deane, a series of lantern slides to illustrate the 'subject. The usual discussion followed, and Mr. Howarth was deservedly congratulated upon his success in treating a somewhat neglected department of entomology in a manner at once clear and interesting.

Miss Parr's Marriage. That the marriage of Miss Parr and' Sir Archer Croft aroused considerable interest in Staunton-on- Arrow, Herefordshire is evident from the following extract from Saturday's " Hereford Times" :—On Tuesday the minds of the parishioners of Staunton-on- Arrow were centred on the wedding of Miss Parr to Sir Archer Croft, and although the service was held at Grappenhall, it was on this, and had been during 'the preceding days, the one topic of conversation. Merry peals were rung on church bells, and the Union Jack floated on the church tower. Mrs. Parr had made arrangements before hand for all the scholars to have an excellent and bountiful tea served in the schoolroom, which had a gay and festive appearance. Among festooned drapery were the mottoes "Welcome" by Miss M. Preece, and " God bless the happy pair," worked in mosaics by Mr. Stirton, which stood out in hold relief. The presents—a silver salver from the Staunton Park tenants, per Mr. Edward Clee ; six silver vases from estate workmen, per Mr. Smallcomb; carriage clock from choir and bellringers, and silver- mounted ebony pin box from school children—had all been gracefully acknowledged by Miss Parr, whe was much touched by such pleasant expressions of good wishes from all classes in the parish. In the . evening a happy throng occupied the schoolroom and dancing was much enjoyed.
