div.head: BREWSTER SESSIONS.
div.p: BREWSTER SESSIONS.
NEW APPLICATIONS AT WARRINGTON.
Another gait for the Magistrates. THE BENCH REFUSE TO ACCEPT. A List of Insanitary Houses.

On Friday last week, the annUal Brewster Sessions for the County Borough of Warrington were held. There was a full bench. Mr. John Fairclough pre- sided, and there were also present: Aldermen Francomb,James Fair dough,andSmethurst,Coun cillors Pierpoint and John Roberts, Messrs. F. Monks, H. Roberts, T. Birchall, S. Wright, R. T. Fairclough, H. Thornton, J. Geddes, J. W. Hayward, C. White, Colonel Ridgway. The Licensing Committee is con- stituted as follows :—Mr. V. Monks, Mr. C. White, Alderman Francomb, Mr. J. Geddes, Councillor Pier- point, Mr. T. Birchall and Dr. Fox. ' There was a large attendance of the general public, and there was an imposing array of legal gentlemen, who appeared in support of a number of new applications. CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT. THE "LONG PULL."

The Chief Constable (Mr. Luke Talbot) in his report to the Justices said :--` I have the honour to submit to you my seventh annual report relative to the busi- ness of the Brewster Sessions, the period dealt with being the year ended December 315t.1902. According to the last census the population of the borough was 64,242. There are in the town 86 alehouses, one less than last year, the licence of the Eagle and Child, Bridge-street, having recently lapsed. There are now practically only 37 beerhouses, as against 39 en the date of my last report, the licences of the Sceptre Inn, Win vick Road, and the Ropemakers' Arms,: Crossley-street, School Brow, having been surrendered I on the 26th inst„ at a special transfer sessions, in con- ' sideration of permission to transfer the Green Dragon alehouse licence to Brooklands, Lovely-lane. This permission was granted to Mr. J. S. Earle, licensee of the Green Dragon,which premises are to be demolished in the course of street improvement. There are 8 off-licences. including shops licensed for the sale by retail of wine and spirits. Total number of licences on the date of this report, 206 ; a proportion of one licence to every 31136 of the population. During the year the police have paid 615 visits of I supervision to licensed premises, and had on 14 occa- sions to caution licensees for slight irregularities' not actually amounting to breaches of the licensing law. NOn the whole, however, the licensed houses have been well conducted. Transfers have been made of 13 ale- house licences, 4 beerhouse licences, and of 16 off licences, a total 'of 33 transfers, as against 28 last , year. Music and dancing licences are in force at 23 alehouses, 7 beerhouses, and 12 otter public rooms not licensed for the sale of intoxicants. For the perfor- mance of stage plays 12 premises are licensed. During the year the magistrates have heard 3.16 charges of drunkenness. 256 of the persons so charged were males, and 83 females. 321 were convicted, and I 18 were cautioned and, discharged. Lost year the charges of drunkenness amounted to 265, showing an increase of 74 during 1902. I attribute this increase, in great measure, to the fact that a large number of men were discharged from military service into the district at the close of the Transvaal War, eachhaving a considerable sum of money at his disposal. Not- withstanding the increase, however, a glance at Table 1 (appended) will show that the number of charges this year is only slightly in excess of the average for the last five years, and below the average for the past decade. Table no. 2 shows the statistics relating to drunkenness for the past year in 18 other towns. In these places the average number of charges was 6.29 per 1,000 of the population. In Warrington it was 527. Of the persons charged with drunkenness in Warrington during the past year, 213 were residents, and 96 were non-residents. Two persons were con- victed 5 times, three persons 4 times, three 3 times, and 14 twice; so that 59 of the charges represent only 22 individuals. There is as yet no local provision of a home for inebriates who might be committed under the Inebri- ate's Act of 1898. In July last I received instructions from the Watch Committee to present to your Wor- ships a report 430 n the alleged abuse in the liquor trade, commonly knownas the" long pull." I accord- ingly made exhaustive inquiries personally, and through my officers, with a view to obtaining reliable information. I also wrote to each licensee within the Borough, asking each to state his individual prac- tice with respect to giving over-measure. I further asked any licensee who might be in thehabit of giving such over-measure to state, in confidence, whether he were compelled to do by stress of competition. The replies to these letters were almost uniform, nearly every licensee stating that he or she gave what is known as the " tot " over and above the standard measure. The " tot " is four fluid ounces. I subse- quently caused a person not connected with the police to purchase, on different dates, a pint of beer at each of 25 licensed houses, belonging to different owners. The beer so procured was measured by the Weights and Measures Inspector immediately after purchase. The result showed that in almost all the cases the vendors had adhered, as near as practicable' to the practice of giving the" tot" (half gill or four fluid ounces) over-measure, the most excessive being two instances where the over-measure was seven fluid ounces above the standard pint. The list of houses where the purchases were made, particulars of the measure, and the certificate of the Weights and Measures Inspector, will be produced in Court, should the Bench wish for more detailed information on this point. My enquiries lead me to believe that the "Long pull" as a. serious or widespread abuse does not exist in the town. Isolated cases there may be where excessive over-measure is given, with a view to attracting custom. It shall be the care of the police to detect and report all such to your worships. The new Licensing Act (1902) came into force on the Ist instant. The Watch Committee have adopted under it a set of regulations relative to the treatment of habitual drunkards. Since the Ist inst. one man has been placed upon what is known as the" Black List." in accordance with the above-nientioned regulations. His photograph and description have been circulated amongst the Licensees of the Borough." THE RENEWAL OF EXISTING LICENCES. THE BENCH AND INSANITARY HOUSES, RENEWALS POSTPONED.

The first business was ahe renewal of existing licences, to which no objection was offered by the police. The Chairman said the Bench had discussed the matter of renewals and there were certain houses which were considered to be insanitary and required alteration. All the licenses would be renewed with the exception of those mentioned in the list which he would read, and -the consideration of those would be adjourned until March 6th in order that inspections might be made. The Chairman then read the list which was as follows : Star and Garter, Friars'-green Bird in Hand, Bank-street Star Inn, Longford-street Red Lion Inn, Winwick-street Brewers' Arms, Winwick-street King's Head, Winwick-street Rope and Anchor, Buttermarket-street Brickmakers' Arms, School-brow Gardeners' Arms, Brick-street Glassmakers' Arms, Brick-street Travellers' Rest, Fennel-street Railway Inn, Knutsford-road Royal Oak Branch, Knutsford-road Roan Cow, Knutsford-road

Adelphi Vaults, Mersey-street Mr. Browne, on behalf of the owners of several of the houses, said they had underconsideration the matter of alteration for two or three months in consequence of a view expressed by certain magistrates. It was pro- posed to submit the plans of the Red Lion, Winwick- road at the adjourned sessions. The Chairman said there would probably be a ,confer- once between the owners of houses and the Licensing Committee.

div.head: HARDY ANNUAL.
div.p: A HARDY ANNUAL.
MR. KEN VON APPLT.ES FOR A FULL LICENCE FOR THE "GREEN MAN."

Mr. F. Monks having taken the chair, Mr. Rigby Swift, barrister (instructed by Mr. Browne) applied on behalf of Mr. Benjamin Kilnyon for a full licence for the "Green Man" Inn. He pointed out that the house was the property of Mrs. Kenyon and Mr. Kenyon had held the licence for a considerable number of years The houseenjoyed the privileges which ware attached to houses licensed for the sale of beer prior to 1869. Mr. Kenyon found in common with other people that his customers required something more than beer, and con- sequently he applied for a full licence and pointed out that the house was not tied. With regard to the re- quirements of the neighbourhood the nearest house in one direction was the Brooklands Hotel, which was 605 yards away. In .the direction of the town the nearest houses were the Bowling Green Inn, 143 yards, and the Ship Inn, 183 yards. The Ship and Bowling Green Inns were very much nearer together than the Green Man and Brooklands. The Railway Hotel was 363 yards away. Within the 400 yards area there were 1543 houses with a population of 8,101 which was equal to about 2,700 per licensed house. As re- garded the wishes of the inhabitants, Mr. Kenyon would tell the Bench that his customers frequently asked him for spirits and regarded it as a hardship that they could not be supplied. Mr. Swift pointed out that if the licence were granted the privileges attacted to an 1869 beerhouse would disappear and the house would be brought more fully under the control of the Bench. Mr. Kenyon wail then called, and said that he had conducted the house for nine years without any com- plaints. Every day people asked him for spirits. Witness was cross-examined by the Chief Constable as to the number of off-licences in the neighbourhood, but Mr. Swift pointed out that it was not suggested that the neighbourhood was not properly supplied with beer. Mr. Knowles, fancy goods dealer and builder, Green- street, presented a, petition in support of the application,

div.head: GREEN DRAGON TRANSFER,
div.p: THE GREEN DRAGON TRANSFER,

Mr. Swift intimated that the application of Mr. James Spencer Earle, for the transfer of the licence of the Green Dragon inn to the Brooklands, of which notice had been given, was withdrawn. This was due to the fact that the transfer had already been granted by the magistrates. ALDERMAN BOLTON AS APPLICANT.
PROPOSED NEW HOTEL IN LOVELY-LANE. OFFER TO SURRENDER THREE LICENCES. BENCH REFUSE TO "PROMOTE HEALTHY RIVALRY."

Mr. Cuthbert Smith, barrister (instructed by Mr. J. Longland) then applied on behalf of Alderman William Bolton for an alehouse licence for a house to be built at the corner of Lovely-lane and Delamere-street. He observed that the applicant had been subjected to some hardship because' the application should have been made at the August sessions, and but for the change in the Licensing Laws, would have been heard at the same tune as the applica- tion for the transfer recently granted by the Bench. Mr. Smith spoke of the applicant's qualifications, and of the manner in which he conducted his houves, point- ing out that the tenants were allowed to sell other bottled beers than those supplied by Mr. Bolton, and were absolutely free in regard to spirits. The nearest fully-licensed house to the site of the proposed hotel was the Brooklands, which was 225 yards away. Other fully-licensed public-houses in the district were the Bowling Green, 564 yards away, and the Railway Inn,l 700. The magistrates had already 'decided that Lovely- lane required a full licence, because they had granted a transfer to Mr. Earle, and the question now became purely one of degree. Was it better that there should be, as there at present was, practically a monopoly on the part of one firm in the district, or that by granting Mr. Bolton a full licence, the Bench should promote—what was always very important in matters of this kind—a certain amount of healthy rivalry between the two? Hesubmitted that it would be better to have two honses,asd the competition would ensure that the quality of the stuff sold in either place was kept up to a reasonable standard. Within a radius of 400 yards of the site there was a population of nearly 8,000. Should the magistrates see their way to give Mr, Bolton a provisional grant for the site and that grant was confirmed he was prepared to give up a fully licensed house in the centre of the town which was do- ing an exceptionally good business—the Exchange Inn —and also to give up the Filecutter's Arms, Fennel-st., which was an 1869 beerhouse, and an off-licence at the corner of Priestley-street and Cartwright-street. If the application were granted the number of licences in War rington would be reduced by two. In each case the licence to be given up was the only licensed house within the 400 yards radius. Mr. Smith frilly described the plans of the proposedhotel and intimated that he could have called witnesses but did not propose to do so. He would also conform to the practice of the Court and not attempt to present any petitions. (Laughter.) Mr. Drury, a well-known figure at Licensing Sessions, went into the witness box and said he had been re- , quested by a number of ratepayers in the district to oppose the application. The people thought that if anyone was worthy of the licence it was Mr. Kenyon. Others said they did not want any spirit licence there. Women who resided in Bostock-street had told him that their husbands were bad enough, now with beer without giving them spirits. (Laughter.) 'Mr. Smith: You speakr on behalf of the ladies do you?
Witness: Yes and the gentlemen too. (Laughter.) Mr. Smith: What committee do you represent? Witness: T represent, myself. (Laughter.) A PECULIAR OP P BEER LICENCE APPLICATION.

Mr, Byrne (instructed by Mr.. R. Evans), made an application on behalf of William Walker of the Albion Mineral Water Works, Frogball-lane for a beer by retail (off) licence. He pointed out that the applicant who was managino, director of M. Walker and Company Limited,alrady possessed an exercise licence which en- titled the firm to sell beer in 41gallon casks and beer in bottles of not less quantity than two dozen reputed quarts. He now desired a licence which would allow them to sell beer in less quantities than that. The Chairman: That would practically make it an off-licence.

Mr, Byrne said there was no difference between an off- licence and that which he was asking for, but his client wonld undertake not to sell any beer on the premises, but would confine himself to the sale of beer on order which would be delivered by the carts when on their rounds with mineral waters,&c. The firm had a number of carts which travelled the country within a radius of seven-or eight or more miles from 'Warrington for the delivery of mineral water syphons. The men had been often asked if they could supply beer in less quantities than two dozen reputed quarts, and it was with the object of meeting this de- mand that the pres9nt application was made: The Chairman: Thervould be nothing to prevent the applicant from supplying one or two or three bottles of beer to anyone who came to the works for them. -
Byrne: There is that danger but if the business is not conducted exactly as the applicant undertook to conduct it, the Bench could at any time take the licence away. - -
The Chairman: My experience is that if you give them a yard they will take two. Mr. Birchall : Does the applicant agree not to sell less than a certain quantity?

Mr. Byrne: He will give you any undertaking of that kind. The object is to supply customers, whilst on their rounds, not to make an off-licence at the works. The firm hadto compete in their business with trades- people from other towns who possessed off-licences and were able to deliver less quantities than the applicant was able to supply with an excise licende. William Walker, the applicant, was then called, and stated that the firm did a business approaching £3,000 or £4,000 a year. TI the application were granted he would undertake not to sell less than one dozen half- pint bottles at a time. He did not want to sell beer other than that which was to be delivered. . Cross-examined by the Chief Constable, witness ad- mitted that he was applying for a licence exactly like an off-licence. He could if he liked if the licence were granted, sell one bottle of beer or half a bottle of beer, at the works, but that was not his intention. The Chairman: He could de that.
The Chief Constable. (to witness): You would probably have five or six carts which would be travelling beer- houses ?--No.

Moses Walker also gave evidence and said he was often asked for dozens of beer, but ho was unable to supply them as the excise licence did not allow him. He found the taste of people was increasing for bottled beer delivered at the houses. This was all the evidence tendered. THE DECISTON.
The magistrates retired to consider their decision. After au absence of five minutes, the Chairman returned and announced that the Bench had decided to refuse all the applications.

Edwardes, Greenheys-road, Liverpool, was found in r back bedroom—presumably that in which he usually slept—lying on a couch with a bullet wound in the fore- head, and beside him an army revolver, with one of the chambers discharged.—it is stated that he had written a letter to his father stating that he would be dead when the letter reached its destination.—The valet was in charge of the house during the absence of the family

div.head: WONDERFUL CASE.
div.p: A WONDERFUL CASE.

They watch their loved ones waste away in the grasp of the terrible monster which hitherto could not be combated. A new light on Diabetes is thrown by the experience of Daniel Healey, 113, Lower Oxford Street, Swansea. He suffered from Diabetes. He went into hospital twice and came out no better. Several doctors attended him and made no progress against the disease. To-day he is well and able to work. The danger that threatened him has. passed. His fellow workmen Are surprised to find him back again at duty,hale and hearty. His cure was Dodd's Kidney Pills, a remedy which is annually becoming wider known in the treatment of all kidney disorders. All sufferers from any weakness should first see the kidneys are well. When a cure is made by Dodd's Kidney Pills of a disease which is the most hopeless stage of kidney weakness, there is hope for all sufferers whose condition is not so acute.

div.head: WARRINGTON SOCIETY.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON SOCIETY.
ANNUAL MEETING AT THE OLD ACADEMY.

The annual meeting of the members of the Warring- ton Society was held at the headquarters, the Old Academy, on Tuesday evening, Mr. J. A. Ewart presid- ing. There were also present :—Messrs. John Fair- hurst, R. Garnett, T. J. Lee, J. Birtles, J. H. Smethurst, B. S. Newcombe, J. Dimmelow, J. Longland, E. V. Walker, H. S. Page, T. Gibson, C. Madeley, with Messrs. Bennett and Hall (hon. secretaries), _

div.head: ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: ANNUAL REPORT.

Mr. BEs.MTETT read the fourth annual report, which was as follows :—"The Warrington Society has signa- lized the year by several great improvements in its venerable home. The Old Academy has been re-roofed, in the old style, at a cost of £42; the members raised a special fund to install the electric light in it; a tele- phone has been provided; and a billiard table subscribed for by a number of the members, which will eventually become the Society's property. The billiard room and the smoke room on the upper floor have been beautifully re-decorated by Mr. J. M. Greenhalgh, free of charge; a flag and staff have been presented, and the long-ex- pected tablet has at last been fixed upon the building. It was unveiled on the 23rd September, by Principal Drummond, of Manchester College, Oxford—the lineal descendant of the Academy; and Mr. Alderman Thomp- , son,Treasurer and Chairman of the Executive of Owens College, Manchester; the Rev. Morley Stevenson,M.A., Principal of the Warrington Training College; and the Rev. E. W. Lummis, M.A.. the minister at Cairo-street (like old John Seddon, the founder, a medallion of whom adorns the tablet) took appropriate part in the proceedings. The tablet was designed by Mr. Albert Warburton, A.R.1.8.A., a member of the Society, and executed by Messrs. Josiah Wedgwood• and Sons, Ltd., of Etruria, the founder of the firm having been one of I the founders and trustees of the Academy, and one of his sons having been educated there. It is hoped that the necessary funds will be forthcoming to enable us to proceed with the erection of another tablet during the coming year, and contributions towards this object will be gratefully received. The Executive have lately learnt with pleasure that Sir Joseph Whitworth, a gunmaker and philanthropist, received a portion of his education in the Academy building, and Mr. R. D. Darbishire,one of his trustees, has shown his interest in the place by a gift of framed photographs of the Rev. Richard Frankland ; of the earliest Academy, which he founded at Rathmell, York- shire in 1685; and of his monument in the Church of St. Alkelda, Giggleswich, with several other rare and highly interesting and unframed photographs. Our records are continually being enriched by some new link in the increasing chain of old association,and since the year began, the Alcove in which Miss Aikin is said to have written some of her poems, and which had apparently been lost sight of, if not forgotten, has been rediscovered in the yard of the adjacent premises off Seddon-place—a pleasing item in a new no- menclature which now commemorates, in Holt- street, Barbauld-street, and Bridgman-street; in Litherla,nd's, in Garnet's, and in Penker's Yards and last, and most significant, perhaps, in Howard- place, the fame of various folks illustrious in the annals of the town, and is itself indicative of the increased regard in which its vanishing traditions have been lately held. The Alcove has,'alas ! been half demolished, but its identity is unmistakable, and we trust that this and other local relics of kindred character will now be lovingly preserved. The Executive observed with pleasure that in Novem- ber last the Rev. Canon Willis read an "Historical Sketch of the Warrington Parish Church," (which,under his enlightened care, has been much improved), before the members of the Warrington Literary and Philo- sophical Society, and heartily welcome this addition to our information concerning the most prominent and con- spicuous building we possess. • The death of Mrs. William Beamont, wife of our first Mayor and greatest antiquarian, is deserving of due mention here; and we sincerely trust that Orford Hall, so long associated with their lives of learning and benevolence, and so rich in memories of old John Black- burne, the distinguished botanist and other famous people, may with its still charming grounds, be long preserved to Warrington, if not, indeed, become the permanent possession of the town. The purchase of a representative picture by our local artist, Henry Woods, R.A., for the Warrington Art Gallery may also here be noted as a pleasing evidence of that increasing pride in the achievements of our fellow- townsmen, which is the object of the Warrington Society to promote, whilst the death of Mr. E. F. Brewtnall is another sad reminder of our local fame in this peculiar field. The reading room at the Academy has been regularly supplied with the following papers: "The Bookman' "The Fortnightly Review, 'The Studio," "The Academy," "The Graphic," "Punch," "The Spectator," "The Sphere," "The Times," "The Warrington Guardian, "The War4ngton Examiner." "The War- rington Observer," and "The Dawn"; and the Execu- tive again desire to acknowledge the receipt of copies of "The British Empire Review," from the British Empire League. The "Book clubs" formed amongst the members still continue, and increase in popularity. The "Club-nights" have been much appreciated. The following was the programme for the year 1902. January 23rd, lecture, "Westminster Abbey," F. C. Larkin. F.R.C.S. England (of Liverpool) ; February 4th, Annual meeting and dinner • February 13th, lecture,' A Warrington Poetess," H. Stuarti Page; February 27th lec- ture, "Switzerland'and Mountaineering," J. A. Ransome ; February 20th, lecture, " The hygienic value of laugh- ter." H. M. Ashton; April 2nd, lecture, "The develop- ment of religion in India," Rev. C. H. Hocken; October 17th, "Alchemy,', J. Rymer Young, F.C.S.; November 6th, lecture, "A night in Roman Warrington," Thomas May, F.E. Inst. Scot.; November 27th. lecture, "Impressions 'of America," C. E. Parker; 27th, 17th, Alpine evening at Parr Hill, Airs. be Blond, and A. H. Crosfield.

On April 12th, the Society paid a most interesting visit (which was arranged by Mr. Charles Madeley) to Chatham's Hospital, Manchester, and were courteously conducted over this delightful relic of the past, with all its picturesque associations, by Mr. Walter T. Browne, the master. The summer excursions were dis- pensed with, mainly on account of the bad weather. ' In September, the Warrington Photographic Society took up its home in the Academy, where a dark room has been specially provided for their use. The Poly- glot Society still find in it a pleasant meeting-place,and carry on a useful work in a delightful way. At the end of the year the Society numbered a hun- dred and nineteen members. It is with great regret that we record the;death of Mr. J. Laverock Tunstall, and the removal from our midst of several prominent old members, including the Rev. F. E. Powell, M.A., and the Rev. C. H. Hocken. The expenses of the Society are heavy, and, if it is to carry out its programme as actively as the Executive desire, its revenues must he considerably increased. It would greatly assist us in establishing the Society upon a sound and permanent basis if it were possible, during 1903, to pay off the I balance due to the bank, which represents what still re- mains unpaid of the cost of furnishing and decorating the Academy. It is not enough that the Executive have been able to provide a pleasant meeting-place for men of kindred tastes, and reverently preserve an I ancient building. They wish to carry out the whole of I the high aims set forth in the preceding pages, and they cordially invite the assistance of all who wish to foster in the town an enlightened spirit of local patriotism, a becoming pride in its distinguished past, and an intelli- gent resolve to win for Warrington, especially in the domain of art and literature, a still more honourable future.

The balance sheet and statement ef accounts showed that the income of the Society amounted to £lll 3s. 2d. and the expenditure £134 16s. Bd. leaving a deficit of £23 16s. 6d. There was also an overdraft at the bank ,of £152 3s. 11d. The assets of the Society were valued lat £203 2s. 4d. and there is also an item of £3O 10s. !which is made up of donations from the guarantors, and Idoes not come under the head of subscriptions.—The report and balance sheet were adopited, and it was left to the. General Purposes Committee to devise a means of raising 'a fund to reduce the bank overdraft and place the Society in a sounder financial condition. The General Purposes Committee was elected, as follows :—Messrs. Fairhurst, Ewart, Madeley, Ashton Page, Lee, Birtles, Wilson, W. Monks, J. Longland, H, Chambers, and B. S. Newcombe. Seven new members were elected, and Mr. C. D. Parkinson, was appointed hon. auditor for the year. Votes of thanks to the Chairman, and the retiring auditor (Mr. Fairhurst), concluded the meeting.

SALVATION ARMY'S BIG SCHEME AT BARROW.— The Barrow officers of the Salvation Army and the divisional committee at Preston are considering a big scheme for providing a new amphitheatre. It was rumoured six months ago that they would purchase the Star Theatre, but this idea fell through, and negotia- tions are now pending for the purchase of a block of dwelling-houses in Dalton-roal, the chief thoroughfare of the borough. The local funds of the Army are in a flourishing condition, and it is anticipated that £5,000 could be readily obtained in twelve months.
FASHIONS OF TO-DAY..

Although the modes are not very progressive at this season (when the rulers of fashion are busily occupied in determining what innovation shall make their debut in a few weeks), there is still much to be seen, admired, and acquired. The terrible period of saletime is happily over, and we are no longer allured against all the promptings of common sense to invest in what are termed, and at first appear to be real "bargains," but more often develop into a species of a "white elephant," and decline to be either ornamental or useful to the unfortunate and rash purchaser. Meantime, the so-called "silly season "ensues and lasts until the spring fashions are fairly launched, and novelties appear on every side.

The buyers from well-known firms are now seeking in Paris and Vienna for all that is chic and likely to suit the taste of everyone. Perhaps the first signs of the coming modes are displayed ix millinery, for the clear sunshine of early spring has an unpleasant trick of revealing the shortcomings of our headgear and encouraging a copse luent desire for something fresh and

div.head: CHARMING 'l(OQ'
div.p: CHARMING 'l(OQ'

dainty. Floral toques are therefore ranch in request and even now there are some very charm- ;ng samples of this style of headgear. The prettiest perhaps are those whose crowns are flat, in fact the plateau shape, the brim being composed of a mass of small flowers of various sorts arranged closely together. A charming toque or hat (as it is difficult to define the difference between- the two) is given in my first illustration. The flat crown is composed of finely pleated creamy tulle, while closely packed pa.rma violets cover the brim, the outlines of which are softened by a drapery of lace which falls half-way down the floral arrange- ment. -In some instances the crown is covered with separate sprays or bunches of the flowers employed to form the brim. Tiny pink and white banksia roses, forget-me-nots or violets are the favourite and most suitable flowers for this kind of headgear. Tulle plays a prominent part in every variety of millinery, and looks very well when covered with a lattice work of black or pale yellow chenille. A striking French model hat had the fiat crown of white astrachan tulle, while the brim was composed entirely of white chenille, long ends of which formed the cache-peigne. It was certainly a very marked style of hat, and could only be recommended to a woman to whose outfit one or more new hats is not a matter for deep consideration' as they are only worn once or twice before being cast aside. Astrachan tulle is one of the prettiest novelties and is made to simulate the fur after which it is named in
ILOUSE,

a wonderful fashion. This is accomplished by clever needle craft in the form of minute gang- jugs and and cleverly manipulated puff jugs. , The pretty blouse depicted has a closely fitting yoke of Irish lace, the lower part con- sisting of tucked and pouched emerald green silk, arranged over a broad swathed band of the silk, which is finished off by little black velvet bows secured in the centre by tiny brilliant buckles. There is something very modish about the blouses which are so fashionable, which ftt closely to the figure at the back but pouch in front over a wide band.

There are already visible signs that short coats coming to a short 'distance above the waist will be much worn when the season is a little more advanced. These are of such a delicate fragile nature thlt they will only be worn over a blouse which harmonizes. I have been permitted a glimpse of one or twe of these dainty little adjuncts of dress, and should counsel all my readers to use up any little odd lengths of piece laca or embroidery, together with any lace edging and accordion pleated chiffon in manufacturing one of these dainty little coats. We are sure to have possessed ourselves of something of the kind at the recent sales. No lining is necessary as the little boleros or lace coatees are only intended to form a finish to a toilette. The simplest are made with a yoke of some fine make of lace such as Valenciennes of a creamy tone with a clear ground sprigged over with flowers. A

COATEE. fall frill of the same kind of lace depends from the yoke. Sometimes narrow WA satin ribbon is inter- threaded, or an edging of irridescent bead-embroidery gives a finish. One I admired was of chiffon, drawn and gauged, and covered with appliques of em- broidered silk flowers.

• The dainty sample sketched is formed of lace, the sleeves which are of the same material coming only to the elbow, from where a deep flounce of the same lace covers the lower part of the arm. A couple of bands of lace insertion finished by paste buckles cross the front of the figure and hold the coatee in place. There are some very fascinating white velvet blouses which are much in vogue this season. These are made very plainly and are devoid of any lace excgpt at the throat and wrists, which, in the first instance, generally takes the form of a cravat avocat of guipure, and in the latter of deep depending ruffles to match. Not for a hundred years has white and its accompaniments of ivory and pale cream been so greatly in vogue as now, and there is every sign of it in- creasing in popularity as the year goes on. It is an extravagant fashion as we all must confess, sad only to be adopted by the very well-to-do, as nothing looks in worse taste or more tm- Itly and unbecoming than a soiled white or coloured gown. Ivory is certainly to be pre. *erred to white for all those who are past that early youth, as it is less trying to. a complain& whiich has lost the fiat bloom. - _

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Among other economies effected at the Royal resi— dences since the accession of the King, is a more care- ful supervision of accounts and supplies from trades— people. It has become the custom to return provisione that are not required, and when without any warning, the Court was detained at Windsor on the day the King and Queen were expected at Chatsworth, the kitchen department at the Castle was thrown into a great state of bustle and excitement. The tradespeople do not like hav!ng their goods returned, and they also complain that the margin of profit now allowed them by the officials is much less than it used to be. All this how- ever merely points to the fact that the household affair% at the Royal residences are being conducted under more careful andiefficient management than was formerly the case. • •
The little son that has been born to the Duke and Duchess of Hamilton is heir not only to the premier
peerage of Scotland, but also to a most imposing array
-of tides beside the dukedom of Hamilton.
He Will bit
a duke, a marquis, and an earl,all several times over, and like the Dllte of Richmond and Gordon, he can claim a. French dukedom in addition to his English and Scotch _ _ _ _
titles. The Duchess of Hamilton was kiss Nina Poore, the sister of Major Poore, who married Lady Flora, the .. __

Duke of HamiltOn's sister, so that the two families' are doubly related by marriage. But though the /infant Marquis of Douglas is born heir to so manytitles,much of the wealth of the Hamiltons was left by the twelfth Duke to his 'daughter, Lady Mary Hamilton, now in her nineteenth year, and who will be one of the most charm- ing of the debutantes to come out this season.

The Duchess of Sutherland will no doubt more than ordinarily appreciate a friendly review of one of her books in which a New York journal refers to the authoress as "Miss Sutherland." The title page bears only the name "Millicent Sutherland," which probably led to this little informality. It however shows that the apprecitative notice is a tribute to the gifted authoress, and not to her high rank in society, and for this reason it will, no doubt, be the more acceptable to the Duchess.

Dr. Elizabeth Blackwell, who lives at Hastings and recently entered upon her eighty second year, was one of the pioneers of feminine ambition, she being the first duly qualified woman doctor. Like all pioneers she had many prejudices and difficulties to overcome, and in America whither she had gone with her family, it was suggested that her only chance of becoming M.D. was to adopt an assumed name, and male attire. She how- ever rejected this idea, and, fighting the battle of her sex, eventually obtained her degree in 1849. After- wards she returned, and entering one of the London hospitals, she was placed on the 'Medical Register" as a duly qualified doctor in 1859. Now that the pantomimes are over, one may be per- mitted to speculate concerning the curious customs of employing women to represent the principal male charac- tersit is only in pantomime that this practice obtains,and if it were adopted in any other plays,it would be objected that it gave the performance an air of unreality. Whatever the merits or demerits may be, the representa- tion of male characters by women affords an indication of the way in which fashions change. When the drama. was developed during the Augustan reign of Queen Elizabeth, the female characters were personated by men, and it would have been thought an impropriety for a woman to appear upon the stage. An unpleasant state of things has arisen at two or three fashionable women's chlbs, when the members and their friends have found it unsafe to leave valuable furs or other belongings about in the, hall, and dressing rooms, owing to the many thefts that have occurred. if these were due to the servants it would no doubt be easy to put a stop to them, but it is well-known that they arise from a dishonest notion of some of the mem- bers that "findings are keepings." Such pilferings are more easy to effect at a woman's than a man's club, and moreover there is the unpleasant fact that the majority; of well-to-do people who suffer from "kleptomania' are women.

The club man simply leaves his overcoat and his umbrella in the hall, whereas a women will perhaps leave a valuable cape, boa, muff, a purse and shopping parcels. Then •it is so easy for the misappropriator to convert such articles of attire to her own use, and unless such pilfering can be stopped, clearly the women's clubs will have to be more particular as to whom they admit within their doors.

The single eyeglass can scarcely be said to enhance anyone's beauty, and it is not likely to be much affected_ by women. Occasionally it is seen in use amongst tu certain class of young men, and there are women who, will go to any length in order to thrust themselves upon other people's notice. Many such as these have of late been trying to make the eyeglass a fashionable distinc- tion in the feminine world, but the attempt will assuredly end in its early retirement. Many fashionable women are wearing with the tea- gown an old lace lappet in the hair, secured by several antique pins, and so arranged as to fall forward over the softly waving tresses. The fashion is a pretty and becoming one, especially to brunettes, but it should be remembered that the lace must be good, nothing cheap or modern being possible for such a purpose. For restaurant and theatre wear,these old world lace lappets appear to be particularly suitable, and those among us who possess such treasures, should* lose no time ie hunting them out, and arranging them to the best ad- vantage. A crossover, a pelerine, or a cape is being built to match each spring costume. The style of these little garments varies considerably, but in no instance do they fall lower than the elbow line. The crossover, which disappears into narrow points at the waist, is finding much favour when soft thin materials are con- cerned; then there is the three-caped tippet, turned back in front to form revers; and again, the little cape with its narrow stole falling in long ends well below the knees. The little pleated sac coat which reaches to the waist only is still worn, but the pelerine, cape, or cross- over will be more modish as the spring advances. The flannel blouse-a one-time hopelessly dawdl garment, and impossible, save for early morning wear— is now donned by quite smart women in the afternoon, with dressy skirts that match in tone exactly. Viyella, in soft shades of green, and mauve, is being extensively' employed for these dainty blouses, a little good lace being the only trimming deemed necessary. Regarding the new designs in Viyella, these are if possible, even more beautiful than ever before, the tones and blending of colors being exquisite.
MADGE.

div.head: FOR FASTER TRAVEL.
div.p: FOR FASTER TRAVEL.

The present year will witness some very interesting developments in locomotion, both on land and by sea. In June next, it is hoped, a portion of the Manchester- Liverpool mono-rail electric express railway will be opened, and that carriages will be running on it at the rate of 110 miles an hour. A promoter is again intro- ducing a bill next se3sion for a London-Brighton mono- rail railway, which would take Londoners down to the sea in half an hour. Some of the leading railway com- panies are electrifying portions of their lines. By the clime of 1903 main-line trains may be running by elec- tricity. There are also to be some novelties in ocean .travel. In May the first turbine steamer driven across Channel will commence running between Dover and Calais. In August another turbino vessel will be placed on the Newhaven-Dieppe service. In April the most powerfully enn'ined liner in the world will start run- ning, Viz., the North German Lloyd "Kaiser Wilhelm der Zweite." She is expected to break the best records on the Atlantic ferry.

We understand that from Monday, 9th inst.,the South Lancashire Tramways Company have arranged with the Great Central Railway Company to book passengers and parcels through by their Electric Cars from Leigh to St. Helens Wigan, Manchester, etc. The traffic will be conveyed by car to Lowton St. Marys, thence by Great Central trains. This, we believe is the first working arrangement between any Electric Tramway Company and a Railway Company. and no doubt the result will be keenly watched from all quarters.

div.head: RU:s7CORN FREE CHURCH COUNCIL.
div.p: RU:s7CORN FREE CHURCH COUNCIL.

The annual meeting of the Free Church Council was held on Friday evening. Mr. D. Bisbrown presided, and there was a fair attendance. A letter was read from the President (Mr. James Pritchard), stating that business engagements in London prevented him from attending. The Rev. Alfred Wells wrote resigning his position as a member of the Council. The Treasurer (Mr. J. M. Frith) submitted a report showing a slight balance in hand. Mr. R. IL Posnett was elected a delegate to attend the Free Church Council meeting at Bristol. A vote of thanks was passed to the retiring officers. The following officers were elected: President, the Rev. T. S. Morris; vice-presidents, the Revs. W. Gay; and R. H. Posnett ; treasurer, Mr. J. M. Frith; secretaries,Messrs. W. Millington and T. Curzon; Mr. A. R. Norman ; addi- tional members on executive, Messrs. F. J. Norman, Gittens, W. Handley, W. Gandy, and Pritchard. The question of offering a passive resistance to the new Education Act was introduced and discussed, but, while no definite decision was arrived at, the Council expressed themselves prepared to stand by their former resolution to enrol the names of members who felt bound to refuse to pay the rates levied under the Act.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must mall cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible,not later than Thursday. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has a much greater chance of insertion than a long one. We cannot under ordinary circumstances undertake to return the manuscripts which are not used.
The " Cowardice " of Gladstone and Chamberlain.

Sir,—ln reply to thei letter of Mr. Joynson Hicks under this head in your last Saturday's issue, and also to one by "Briton ''in the Warrington" Guardian "in which"Briton"admonishes me to add Imperialism to my Liberalism, I thank" Briton" for the suggestion, but I would prefer to be without the adjective until 1 know what it implies. I hold that true Liberalism includes all that is worthy in Imperialism. Before you can determine whether anyone is an Imperialist or not, it is necessary to define what is meant by the term. If Imperialism means a loyalty to our country, and a res- pect for the flag which is her emblem, pride in her his- tory, a glorying in the fact that she has carried the blessings of Christianity, freedom, justice civilization and self-government where ever the flag has been plan- ted; if it means an intense desire to extend these bless- ings to all who come wider our rule, and to hold them as a sacred trust for those who come after us—then I claim to be an Imperialist of the Imperialists. But if, on the other hand, it includes a lust of empire, a desire for territory which belongs to others, a backing of the country whether it is right or wrong' then I repudiate the term and will not add it to my Liberalism, for the two principles must ever oppose. " Briton " says we are beginning to respect the flag, and even to discover that our enemies are not always in the right." Indeed, and who does "we" include, and when did we begin to respect the flag? If "Briton is one of those who is only beginning, then.l claim that my Imperialism, or rather patriotism is of much older growth than his. The essential difference between Liberal patriotism, and .the imperialism represented by Con- servatives of the type of Mr. Joynson-Hicks is revealed in Mr. Joynson-Hicks own words, where he says" If Sir, there is one fault which I possess to an exaggerated degree it is a fervent patriotism, and rightly or wrongly (the emphases are mine) I would support my country against all comers." Here then we have indicated the clear line of cleavage betwe'm a true patriotism and the false imperfect type. A true patriot will support his country only when right, and strive to restrain it when wrong. Right must stand before patriotism, or rather the truest patriotism must be founded on the right. It is an easy thing to shout "Rule Britania," "My country right or wrong." It is a more difficult, but a more worthy attitude to take. while willing to sacrifice all for the country when it is in the right, to oppose it at all cost when in the wrong. The fault of which Mr. Joynson-Hicks accuses.himself is one that is not confined to himself, but permeates and vitiates much of the so called Imperialism "Briton" speaks of the humiliation after Majuba. Now, what are the facts? Some time prior to this battle the English Government had realized, that, as Mr. Fitz- patrick in his "Transvaal from within" admits Shop- stone "had rushed the annexation" and that the Boer Republic has been annexed,not as it was then thought, with the consent of the Boers but against the wishes of the great majority. Lord Kimberley who had been ne- gotiating since January 11th, telegraphed to General Colley, that if the Boers ceased fighting, commissioners would be appointed to arrange a settlement. General Colley accordingly wrote to Mr. Kruger on February 21st, stipulating for an answer within forty-eight hours. Unfortunately Mr. Kruger had left the Boer camp on a journey, so that the letter did not reach him in time, and General Colley, thinking his proposal rejected, de- cided to advance and occupy Majuba, with the result we all know. From this it is clear, that the peace made with the Boers as I stated in my last had nothing to do with Majuba, as Mr. Joynson-Hitiks and "Briton" seem to think. The pertinent question is, should Mr. Glad- stone's Government have been turned aside from its intention to restore to the Boers their self-government, because Colley with 627 troops was driven with loss from the top of Majuba by about 1,000 Boers? Should they have taken vengeance on the Boers? No doubt Mr. Joynson-Hicks and "Briton" would say yes. They would not have called it vengeance but given it some pretty name, and made it masquerade in the robes of firmness, justice etc. It may be an unpopular stand to take—to this I am indifferent—but the very thing that these gentlemen look upon as a sign of cowardice on the part of Mr. Gladstone's GOvernment,l hold to be an act of the bravest self restraint. To have turned away from their purposes because of the reverse of Majuba,to have allowed their policy to be overborne by the awakened lower passions of the nation, to have accepted guidance from those who considered force the only remedy,would have been to act the part of cowards and traitors to the nation's highest interests. lam not here dealing with :the larger question of the wisdom of the general policy in giving back self-government to the Boers, subject to the suzerainty of the Queen. That point lam quite ready to discuss with Mr. Joynson-Hicks oranyone else,but for the present it would take us too far afield. I here desire to limit the question to the "cowardice" of Gladstone's Government in connection with Majuba. am interested in reading the extract which Mr. Joynson-Hicks gives from the speech of Lord Ki mberley, and I admire its sound sense. Mr. Hicks will find similar arguments in Mr. Chamberlain's speeches about 'the same date, in which he dwells not only on the moral laspects of the question, but on the material onesas well, and shows that, after a vast outpouring of blood and treasure in subduing the country, we should have to keep an armed garrison of English troops permanently stationed in the Transvaal to hold the country by force against the will of the inhabitants. The false statement definitely declared, or clearly implied that the policy was the result of Majuba and the work of cowardice, has done service at hundreds of Conservative meetings beforelit appeared in Warrington in public meeting and in public press. It is time some of these. false state- ments and implications were nailed to the counter. "Briton" seems to be surprised that I should defend Mr. Chamberlain against the charge of cowardice made against the men forming the Gladstone Government of 1881. Surely the fact that Mr. Chamberlain has altered his party adhesion should not influence me in defending a brave man, when I consider him attacked, any more than it prevents rue wishing him success in his present difficult mission. Our politics have not sunk so lowthat any of us should hesitate in doing justice to a political opponent. I have just been perusing the despatches prior to the last war. They are melancholy reading. Now that so much misrepresentation has been cleared away, and wet can see with a clearer vision, we come to the same con- clusion that Mr. Chamberlain has lately expressed in regard to the misunderstanding on both sides. It was unfortunate, that on our side, we had such a pugnacious controversialist as the mouth-piece of our diplomacy, in the person of Mr. Chamberlain, and on the other hand, it was unfortunate for the Boers that they had at their head a shrewd but somewhat stupid, suspicious, and haggling personage—Paul Kruger. Still., I very much doubt, with other representatives conducting the negotiations whether,it would in the long run have pre- vented a conflict. The racial cleavage,the conflicts ofa cen- tury, the wide gap in the two civilizations, and last, but not least, the distrust engendered by the Jameson Raid, all made for war. Be that as it may, I do not wonder, that Mr. Crosfleld should speak strongly about the manner of Mr. Chamberlain's diplomacy. As a fighter, Mr. Chamberlain is at his best, he is no coward what- ever the odds and he never has been one whatever Mr Joynson-Hicks may imply to the contrary. But as a diplomatist, where consideration for the feelings, and even prejudices Of opponents have to be considered and humoured, Mr. Chamberlain is at his worst. I did not keep copies of Mr. Crosfield's speeches, but if he has spoken strongly about the Jameson Raid and Mr. Chamberlain's style of diplomacy, I am quite with hint Mr. Joynson-Hicks', reproof to Mr. Croslield of what he absurdly calls "mu veiled charge Of wholesale murder against the Colonial Secretary" comes ill, from one who but a week before, ascribed the cause of the war' and that unjustly,to the cowardice of Mr. Gladstone's Government. The proverbial pot once more calls the kettle black.—Yours truly, CHARLES E. PARKER.

February 12th, 1903. P.S. I notice Mr. Joynson-Hicks speaks of my "per- sonal abuse." I seenothing in my letter to which such a term can, in any fairness, be applied, and I am sorry that Mr. Joynson-Hicks should think that such was in any way intended.

div.head: Examiner, Friday, February 13, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Friday, February 13, 1903.
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL AND THE EDUCATION ACT. The Constitution of the New Committee. A Draft Scheme Prepared.

A summons has been issued to the members of the Warrington Town Council requesting their attendance at a special meeting of the Council to be held on Tues- day evening next for the purpose of making a scheme to establish and constitute an Education Committee for the Borough. The Museum Committee has prepared a draft scheme which will be submitted to the Council for confirma- tion.

div.head: CONSTITUTION OF THE COMMITTEE.
div.p: CONSTITUTION OF THE COMMITTEE.

It is proposed by the Museum Committee that (1). There shall be constituted for all purposes of the Education Act 1902 a committee consisting of 22 persons of whom 12 (including the Mayor and the chairman of the Finance and Estate Committee for the time being) shall be members of the Council,and shall be called representative members, and 10 other persons appointed who shall be called co-optative members. • (2). Every representative member shall be appointed to otfice for the term of 3 years reckoned from the date of his appointment. (3.) The Co-optative members shall be competent persons of experience in education or acquainted with the needs of the various kinds of schools in the Borough, and shall be appointed after consideration by the Council of recommendations from the following bodies in the following proportions that is to say One by some duly constituted association represent- ing Church. of England - Voluntary Schools in the Borough. One by some dilly constituted association representing Roman Catholic Voluntary Schools in the Borough. One by some duly constituted association representing Nonconformist and Unsectarian Voluntary Schools in the Borough. One by.the Governors of the Warrington Grammar School.
One (a -woman) by the Council of the Warrington Diocesan Training college. . . . .
One by theWariingtoriChamber of Commerce. One by the Workingmen's Committee of the Warring- ton Infirmary. Three by the Education Committee. _ _ _

The persons to be recommended by the Education Committee nuist be persons experienced in education other than elementary. (4.) The Council shall appoint three members of the Technical Instruction Sub-Committee for the Borough existing at the date of this scheme members of the first Committee who at the expiration of the term for which they are appointed shall be eligible for re-appointment either as representative or co-optative members as pro- vided by this scheme.

(5.) Every co-optative member shall be appointed to office for the term of three years reckoned from the date of the appointment. (6.) The Town Clerk shall forthwith after the date of this scheme forward a copy thereof to the several personsacting as secretaries or other authorised officers of the bodies referred to in paragraph 3. (7.) Whenever a recommendation for appointment of a person as a member of the committee has been made the person acting for the time beingas the secre- tary or other authorised officer of the body so recom- mending shall by writing under his hand certify such recommendation to the Council and shall forthwith transmit the certificate to the Town Clerk. In the event of any of the said bodies failing to make and certify in manner aforesaid any recommendation within 21 days after notice in writing to the person actin,* as their secretary or other authorised officer so to do from the Council under the hand of the Town Clerk the Council shall forthwith appoint such person to supply the vacancy as the Council shall think fit. (8.) If a representative member ceases to be a mem- ber of the Council he shall cease to be a member of the committee.
(9.) If a co-optative member ceases to be a member of the body by whom he was recommendedhe shall cease to be a member of the committee.
(10.) If a co-optative member shall become a mem- ber of the Council he shall cease to be a member of the committee.

(11.) in case any of the bodies referred to in para- graph 3 shall cease to exist, the person appointed on the recommendation of such body shall cease to ,be a member of the committee and the Council shall there- upon appoint such person to fill the vacancy as they shall think fit.
(12.) No person shall be appointed a Co-optative member if he holds an office of profit in a school or college provided or maintained by the Committee or the Council. •

(13.) Every Co-optative member shall at or before the first meeting which he attends upon his first or any subsequent entry into office signa memorandum eeclar- ing his acceptance of the office of member and his will - ingness to act in the purposes of this scheme and until he has signed such a memorandum he shall not be en- titled to discharge the. functions of a member.

div.head: VACANCIES.
div.p: VACANCIES.

(14.) A member of the committee may resign on. giving to the Town Clerk notice in writing of his inten- tion of doing so, and a casual vacancy on the committee shall thereupon occur. (15.) If a member of the committee absents himself during six successive calendar months from all meetings of the committee except from temporary illnessor other cause to be approved by the committee such person shall cease to be a member of the committee and a casual vacancy on the committee shall thereupon occur. (16.) If any casual vacancy on the, committee occurs by death, resignation, or otherwise, the committee shall appoint a person to fill the vacancy in the same manner and on consideration of the like recommendation (if any) as the appointment of the person whose death, resignation, or disqualification has caused the vacancy was made, and the person appointed to fill such vacancy shall continue in office so long only as the person in whose place he is appointed would have continued in office.

(17.) Any co-optative member who is declared bank- rupt or compounds by deed with his creditors or makes an arrangement or composition with his creditors uuder the Bankruptcy Act by deed or otherwise or who shall become disqualified or incapacitated to act shall there- upon forthwith cease to be a member of the committee. (18.) Whenever a vacancy occurs the committee shall cause an entry to be made in the minute book of such vacancy and notice of such vacancy shall as soon as conveniently may be given to the Council or to the Secretary or other authorised officer of the body who recommended the member causing such vacancy. (19.) The powers under the Technical Instruction Acts 1889 and 1891 vested in or delegated by the Coun- cil on the 10th day of November last to the Museum Committee or the Technical Instruction Sub-Committee shall cease on the date of this scheme.

(20.) The committee at their first meeting and after- wards annually shall appoint members to be the Chair- man and Deputy-Chairman respectively. (21.) The quorum of the committee shall be 5. (22.) The first committee shall be appointed by the Council at their first available ordinary meeting after the date of this scheme.

(23.) The Town Clerk shall convene the first meeting of the committee within fourteen days. after their appointment by notice in writing addressed and posted to each member at least two clear days before such meeting. (24.) The committee shall in the month of (February) in each year, or oftener if required by the Council, fur- nish to the Council a full detailed estimate of expendi- ture receipts and liabilities on capital and revenue accounts and of probable loan requirements during the ensuing financial year, or for such other period as the Council may require and such estimate shall be in such form and shall contain such information as the Council shall from time ta time require. (25.) The date of this Scheme shall be the day on which the Board of Education declare their 'approval of it.

div.head: SOUTHWARK POISON CASE. " Chapman " Committed on Three Charges.
div.p: SOUTHWARK POISON CASE. " Chapman " Committed on Three Charges.

For the seventeenth and the last time Severin Kloso- wski, also knownas George Chapman, late of the Crown, in Borough High-street, appeared on Wednesday at the I Southwark Police-court to answer the charge of having I wilfully murdered Mary Isabella Spink, Bessie Taylor, and Maud Eliza Marsh by the administration of poison. • The prisoner was accompanied by two stalwart warders from Brixton Prison, who sat with him in the dock during the very brief proceedings. Mr. Sims, who appeared for the Treasury, said that since the last hearing,the prosecution had had the oppor- tunity of considering the evidence which might be j given by the three medical men whom Dr. Stoker con- suited in the case of Bessie Taylor, and they did not propose to present it at that Court. If it was deemed necessary elsewhere the defence would have due notice. He had now to ask for the committal of the prisoner on the.three charges of wilful murder. The Magistrate (Mr. Cecil Chapman), addressing the prisoner, asked him whether, having heard the evidence. he wished to make any statement or to call any wit- nesses. Chapman made no reply, but Mr. Sidney, his solici- tor, said that he would plead not guilty, reserve his defence, and call no witnesses. The prisoner was then formally committed to take his trial on the three charges at the next sessions of the Central Criminal Court. As he left the dock he was greeted with a volley of hisses from the crowded court.

Tt is stated that Mr. Justice Grantham, who has this week returned from circuit, but who goes back again to the assizes at Liverpool next week, will on his return to London be the judge sitting at the next Central Criminal Court, when the case of Chapman, charged with the murder of Maud Marsh and others, will come before him.

The Provision of Municipal Bowling
Greens.
Alderman Bolton CritiCiS2l.
The monthly meeting of the Warrington. Trades and Labour Council was held in Cairo-street Schools on TuAsday evening, Mr. J. Edwardson presiding over a good attendance of delegates.

div.head: VOTE OF CONDOLENCE.
div.p: VOTE OF CONDOLENCE.

The CHAIRMAN informed the Council of the death of Mrs.lGeor"e Willcocks, wife of one of tbedelentes,and moved a vote of condolence with Mr. Willcoc6ks in his bereavement. ' The SECRETARY seconded and the motion was carried in silence.
PLACE OF 'MEETING.
The SECRETARY remarked that that was the last meet- ing to be held in that room as the Council would in future meet in Bold-street Wesleyan School.
THE VISIT OF THE PENRHYN CHOIR

The SEcRETARY.said he had been unable-i-o.prepare a balance as all the proceeds of the sale of tickets had not yet been received, but he expacted that the amount realized by this concert would be over £2O.

div.head: CHARITY ORG ANIZAT lON SOCIETY.
div.p: THE CHARITY ORG ANIZAT lON SOCIETY.

The SECRETARY said he -r-EQ.;;;i4--ii--letster from Captain G. R. Crosfield informing him of the meeting which was held at the Town Hall on January 16th in regard to the proposed formation of a local branch of the Charity Organization Society. Miss Broadbent who was the prime; mover in the matter, had asked him (Captain Crosfield) to invite representatives of one or two trade union societies and benefit societies, and he wished to know if Mr. Stott cluld find out who would be willing to act on the committee. He (Mr. Stott) replied stating that the time was rather too short to make arrangements for representatives of tiade organ- izations to attend the meeting,and he had written to Mr. David Houghton in regard to the suggestion that friendly societies should be represented. It was impossible for him to attend the meeting and subse- quently he received a letter from Miss Broadbent informing him that he had been electeda member of the Provisional Committee. He replied regretting his inability to attend the meetings owing to the time for which they were 11xed,and expressing the opinion that if any money could be saved which had been wasted by charity organizations overlapping it would be of advant- age to the town generally. It was decided that the names of Messrs.Plinston and Malone be submitted to the committee as the delegates to represent the Trades Council. THE DENARY _MINERS'_ DISPUTE. .

A letter was received from the Leicester Trades Council appealing for subscriptions to aid the men, women and children who had been turned out of their homes in the depth of winter in consequence of this dispute. After some discussion it was decided not to enter- tain the appeal.
THE PROVISION OF MUNICIPAL BOWLING GREENS. ALDERMAN BOLTON CRITICISED.

The SECRETARY read a letter from the-fo-wn Clerk in reference to the provision of municipal bowling greens' which stated that the Town Hall, Park and Baths Com- mittee could not see their wayto recommend the Coun- cil to entertain the proposal. Mr. PODMORE said he understood the letter was hardly up-to-date. There had been'a discussion in the Town Council, and they found a practically unanimous feeling in favour of the provision of public bowling greens. (Hear, hear). He was very pleased to see the efforts on behalf of the proposal made by various coun- cillors in their "Borough Home," and particularly by Councillor James Evans. They had a peculiar example of municipal wisdom from Alderman Bolton. One hardly knew what to say about Alderman Bolton. He had been;told since that they never knew how to take the Alderman, whether seriously, or whether he meant what he said as a joke. (Laughter.) He thought they had better take the latter interpretation, because he thought Alderman Bolton was joking when he made a statement that grass would not grow in Warrington and that it would cost £2,000 to establish municipal bowling greens. One would imaginethat he was in practice so that the next time Ohmy's circus came he could take the position of a clown. (Laughter.) Certainly he had made himself a laughing stock in Warrington as far as his (the speaker's) experience went. He thought that if Alderman Bolton, having had his little joke, would seriously consider the matter, and take the initiative in bringing about the provision of one or two bowling greens in Warrington, it would do him more good, from a public point of view, than any joke of that descrip- tion he might like to perpetrate. tHear, hear). He (the speaker) was in hopes that before a year had elapsed they would have a municipal :bowling green in Warrington, which would afford the working classes opportunities of recreation. The CHAIRMAN considered that Springffeld would be a good place for a bowling green but said there ought also to be greens in each of the parks.

div.head: TaF, U.NMIPLOVED.
div.p: TaF, U.NMIPLOVED.

The SECRETARY said the Town Clerk wrote to him acknewledging the receipt of a letter on the above sub- ject and stating that he would be glad to know approximately the number of men belonging to trade unions who were out of employment. He (Mr. Stott) sent postcards to each Trade Union branch asking for the required information. He received information from ten branches and forwarded it to the Town Clerk Tt appeared. that on an average about 8 or 9 per cent of the members were unemployed. Some societies had only one per cent out, of work,whilst other had between 20 and 30 per cent. The Ironworkers' Society had no members actually unemployed at the present time but some members were in a worse position than many trade unionists who were not working because they had done only about two " turns " per week for the past two years. On some occasions men had been actually without work for five or six weeks. It would therefore be seen that the conditions of employment in the iron trade were at i present very bad. It was n the building trade that the highest percentage of members were unemployed, the figure beings between 20 and 30 per cent. The TOWN CLERK replied to him as follows :—''T am obliged for your letter of the 6th instant. The inform- ation received by you tallies with information I obtained from other sources. lam glad to find that the conditions of employment are not so serious as was at first antici- pated. I quite agree that it is most desirable that a scheme of a permanent character should be established in all centres of industry so that in times of distress through lack of employmant steps might be taken to provide work or to give relief in same form without disfranchising the recipients. I have received notice of a conference on the problem of unemployment which is to be held in London on the 27th. The Presi- dent of the Association of Municipal Corporations will be the Chairman. T shall ask the Council to allow me to attend the Conference and T. hope some practical scheme will be devised, preferably by national organiza- tion, to deal with the .difticulties which at the present time the local authorities are unable to remove." The SECRETARY said he .thought the Town .Clerk had interpretedtheir views very clearly. They wanted the Council to establish some permanent method of reliev- ing the unemployed in tunes of distress. Mr. PODMORE considered the letter from the Town Clerk was quite a treat. They usually received such abrupt.to—the—point letters that when the Town Clerk gave them explanations or an expression of opinion such as was contained in the letter it was very interesting to them. Now that the Association of Municipal Corpora- tions was taking the unemPloyed question np,he thought there was hope that information would be obtained which would lead to a great deal of good being done in the future. He had great hopes that the municipalities of the country would play a great part In facing and dealing with rimy problems which effected the work- ing classss and in fact all classes.

div.head: PROPOSED TRADES HALT, TN WA RRTNGTON.
div.p: THE PROPOSED TRADES HALT, TN WA RRTNGTON.

The SECRETARY reported that the Executive Com- mittee met to discuss this proposal and had decided to recommend that a &mutation from the Council should inspect the textile halls at Bolton and Heywood before particulars of the schema were submitted to the branches. They had yet no idea as to tha size of the hall they would require, or as to the amount of ground rent and the cost of management. Mr. Stott gave particulars as to the cost of the establishment and maintenance of halls in other towns, and said the question at present was whether they thought there was sufficient public spirit among Warrington trade unionists to build a hall and support it in such a manner as would enable it to be carried on efficiently. He thought it would be ad- vantageous to co-operate with the Friendly Societies, and with regard to the size of the hall, the committee thought that a hall was required in Warrington smaller than Parr Hall and larger than the Co-operative Hall. It would be advisable for the Council to ascertain the extent of the support they might expect from the branches. Many branches preferred meeting at public houses and if those conditions were going to obtain it would be a bad look out for a trades hall. He did not, however, want to damp the ardour of those who were greatly in favour of the hall. The CHAIRMAN said the society he represented was strongly in favourpf the hall and would no doubt take nn some shares. No doubt individual members would also take shares.
It was decidefi that Vessrs. Buckley, Stott, and Potts should inspect the halls at Heywood and Bolton.
PROPOSED LABOUR BUREAU.

The SECRETARYsuggested that the Town Council should be asked to receive a deputation to advocate the establishment of a labour bureau. He considered that a bureau would be an advantage to trade unionists and particularly to unskilled labourers. They would be able to form an estimate of the extent of thennemploy- ment in the town. The money spent on the establish- ment of the bureau would not be wasted as business men would benefit by it in addition to the workmen. _ _ .

Mr. KF.Nnrucx cnnsidered that a bureau would not be of any benefit to trade unionists. Mr. BUCKLEY said that so long as they had a Town Council mainly composed of capitalists and employers of labour the bureau would be used for the purpose of obtaining cheap labour. They had not a single labour representative on the Council and he was in favour of the question being deferred until they gotlabour repre- sentatives. There were other things in Warrington which would benefit the working classes more than a
labour bureau. Too many Corporation contracts were let out to unfair firms and they would be unable to stop this until they had representatives on the Council.

Mr. PussToN proposed that the matter be deferred— he would not say whether for six months or for six thousand years. (Laughter.) He considered that Trade Unionists would not derive any more benefit from the bureau than if they had a master who entirely dis- approved of trade union principles.. •

PODAIORE seconded and said that if the Town Clerk couldprevail upon the Council to permit him to attend the conference in connection with the unem- ployed question he would undertake to say that labour bureaux would form a parminent subject of discussion. The Council were watching the pennies now, they had detectives on the job—(laughter)—and they had not to send too many deputations now that there were repre- sentatives of the Non-Trading party on the Council. If the Town Clerk went to the conference he would learn a great deal, he had no doubt, about labour bureaux. It was decided to defer the matter.
