div.head: WORKING OF THE EDUCATION ACT.
div.p: THE WORKING OF THE EDUCATION ACT.

The SECRETARY said that at a future meeting the Council ought to discuss a question of very great im- portance—the representation of the Council on the new education authority. In Liverpool it was proposed that the Trades Council should have the option of nominating one representative on the committee and in Manchester a scheme had been passed recommending that delegates from the Trades Council and Women's Trade Union Council should be placed on the committee. He had pleasure in moving that he (Mr. Stott) be in- structed to write to the Town Council asking for per- mission for the Trades Council to nominate one mem- ber of the new authority. Mr. PLINSTON said it was of the utmost importance that the Council should endeavour in the interests of those whom they represented to secure representation upon tbe committee. The motion was agreed to. The SECRETARY said he had received a letter from the Women's Local Government Society asking the Council to request the Borough member to support a measure which would be introduced into Parliament to make it possible for women to be elected onCountyand County Borough Councils so as to allow them to be elected on the local education authority.
Mr. PLINSTON said he would like to know how much had been expended on stamps and stationery in writing to the Borough member, and the amount of profit or loss incurred. . (Laughter.)

, The SECRETARY: It is not much. Mr. PODMORE Moved that the Secretary write to Mr. Pierpoint. Mr. PLINSTON said he did not believe in wasting stamps and stationery on a member of Parliament whose vote had never been of any service to any resolution they had asked him to support. The motion was carried.

div.head: WOKKS ACCIDENT.
div.p: A WOKKS ACCIDENT.
Warrington Man is Awariieri £l5O Damages.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday the hearing was concluded of the claim made under the Employers Liability Act by William Salt, of 11, Mill- lane, against the St. Helens Cable Company, for £202 damages for the loss of four fingers from his right hand whilst following his employment at the company's works at Warrington on August 23rd.—Mr. Cuthbert- Smith, barrister (instructed by Mr.' Steel) again appeared for the applicant and Mr. Browne represented the defendant company. At the last hearing of the case, Mr. Smith pointed out that the grounds on whieh the applicant sought to recover, were that the place on which he had to stand whilst working at machinery was insecure and did not afford a firm foothold, and also that the machinery was dangerous and not properly fenced. The applicant was making a cab tyre and was putting rubber between the cylinders of the "warming up" machine when the boards on which he was "standing tilted, and he was thrown forward, his hand going between the rollers. The consequences were that half of the hand had to be amputated. Befere the accident. Major Roe, H.M. Inspector of factories, visited the works. Thelbspector considered the machine dangerous and was heard to advise that a bar be placed in front of the machine to prevent anyone falling for- ward. No bar, had, .however, been placed there, and another workman alleged that ha was caught in the machinery some time after the present accident, his shirt being torn off. At' the outset of the resumed hearing on Thursday, Mr. Browne read letters which his clients had sent to the plaintiff in which they stated they were willing to ry-ty half the average earnings of the plaintiff under the Workmen's Compensation Act. This offer was refused.

Mr. Smith, in answer to His Honour, stated that the plaintiff claimed £202, but he accepted the wages book produced by the defendants showing that the plaintiff had been receiving about £53 a year. He agreed to the claim being reduced to £l6O. Mr. Browne observed that was the maximum which could be claimed if the plaintiff had been killed. He could not claim more than that under the act. Continuing Mr. ,Browne Pointed out that the machine in question was a simple looking one, and he had ample evidence to prove that it was not dangerous. He would like his Honour to go down to the works and see it. His HONOUR expressed his willingness to ' go to the works.

Mr. Browne said he based his defence on the grounds (1), that the ways were not defective, (2) that there was no negligence on the part of defendants, (3) that the machine was not dangerous, (4) that the platform was not supplied by the defendants but by the plaintiff, who was, therefore, responsible, and, (5) that the plaintiff was negligent in the conduct of his work by putting his fingers too close to the machine. The first witness called for the defence was George Price, manager of the_ mixing department of the St. Helens Cable Company,who said he had had 18 years' ex- perience in the business.He had never seen albar across a machine like the one in question. it was not a dangerous machine; it was perfectlysafe. The workmen objected to a bar, which would be a source of danger, in his opinion,because the workmen would have to get underiit to place the rubber in the machine and was liable to catch his head. it depended on the height of a man as to whether a platform was necessary. Plaintiff would not require one, but he pleased himself whether he had one or not.—Cross-examined by Mr. Smith, witness said the platform plaintiff used was not a proper one. He knew of three similar accidents from personal know- ledge. He disagreed with the remark of Major Roe that the machine was dangerous. At this stage of the proceedings. His Honour, accom- panied by MI.. Cuthbert Smith, Mr. Browne and Mr. Price proceeded to the works of the defendants to view the machine. On their return - -

William Goodie. of 67, Baxter-street. stated that he had been 12 years in the trade and had worked at the machine in question. No platform was needed to stand on unless th,. man working the machine wts very small. He personally worked without a platform.—Cross-ex- amined: He considered this class of machine was dangerous but he did not think it could be made any safer than it was.

John Worthington, foreman of the mixing department. said the plaintiff had never complained to him of the danger of the platform or the danger of the machine. The platform WAS in front of the machine when Salt started. If the plaintiff did not like it all he had to do was to throw it on one side. The company didnot provide the platform.—Oross-examined: It was quite possible that the plaintiff had made a statement to him resPect- ing the dangerous nature of the floor. There was no difficulty in working a washing machine witha bar across' but that was owing to it being smaller than a "warmer- no," and the quantity lifted into the machine was much smaller. - -

John Bolton, rubber mixer, 7, Oldham:street. Latch- ford, gave evidence as to drawing the plaintiff out of the machine. He could not work the machine with a bar across, and had not seen one across in his "LS experience.—Cross-xamined : Salt was not working the machine regularly. He considered it dangerous. "7ames Lewis stated that he had had 22 years' experi- ence with these machines, He had seen machines with bars across, but he preferred the Machine without. William Henry Egerton, 27, Victoria-street, said he ha. 4 worked a machine with a bar across, and he con- sidered it more dangerous than if it were without one, as the workman was liable to catch his head against it. —Cross-examined: He had himself lost fingers through a similar accident.

His Honour held that the ways were defective owing to the negligence of the defendants and that the acci- dent, happened in consequence, without any contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff. 'the planks of the platform were defective according to the evidence of everybody, and the defendants were negligent in supplying them and allowing them to be used. He must decide against the defendants and award the plain- tiff 2150.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
By " Ovalist."

The ill-luck o 4 the Warringtouians was again mani- fested on Saturday, when they had to tackle the power- ful Salford team, minus Isherwood, Fish, Dickenson, and Burgess, the men who are the mainstay of the back division. Can it be wondered at, therefore, that Warrington lost? What hope was there with such a scratch fifteen as was put in the field ? As a matter of fact there wtis ground for not a little hopefulness. The fifteen were all triers,. and none of them were novices, while at three-quarter time they were making such a good fight of it that the odds were slightly against the visitors. Then Warrington's bad luck manifested itself,the chance of the day going Salford's way instead of ours, and the doom of the homesters was sealed. Bell intercepted a pass, got' clear away, and put 5 points on the score, an exact repetition of Dickenson's . performance last season, which is about all the compensation Warrington have up to this happening on Saturday. Warrington were only one point behind, and peppering the,- Salford line most determinedly. Afterwards they gave in, and Messer got a third final try which completed Warring- ton's discomfiture by 11 points to 2 points.

There is no doubt that Salford were the better team, but the better team does not always win and their ultimate success was very thubtful without the slice of luck which came in Bell's way. He turned it to fine ac-.:ount, 'tis true, and the effort was a good one individually, but the opportunity was luck 'pure and simple. The Warrington lads made a gallant fight against big odds and big opponents, and though Salford continually got the ball,they were most •effectwely Waled. At three-quarter they were very little superior to the home reserves, and, but for the übiquitous Lomas their scoring power mould have been infinitesimal. He had to make all the running and his play was an example of what one class half- back can do for a team. Norris, on the right, a big and powerful player, made some strong runs, but was always well tackled, the other three-quarters being nuderate. Dan Smith, in the rear was, however, excellent, he and Hallam both giving a fine display. The home backs all did well though they ware mostly defending, and no fault could be found with their display under the circumstances. Forster had hard luck more than once in not scoring, while Harris was neglected. Little , Edmunds was everywhere, and but for that one fatal pass which went to Bell, he played brilliantly, and worried the Reds more than a little. Warrington sadly missed the regular centres, whose presence would have had a big effect on the mime even though the forwards were quite out- • 0 „, classed.

The League results were generally surprising last Saturday; -for Broughton Rangers went under to ilunslet on their own sacred turf," Ahr Albert " kick- ing the goal which won his side the match. Swinton also dropped a point at home, where Kingston Rovers played .with much dash in weather which suited them better than their opponents. Halifax defeated HUdders- field comfortably and are again at the head of affairs, while Runcorn trounced St. Helens and Oldham accounted for Wigan.
The League table up to date is as follows For Agst. -

The South-West Lancashire Competition is almost as open as the League for four out of six clubs at present stand a chance for the cup. Runcorn are, at the head of affairs and have a record superior to . any of the others, but Leigh, Warrington, and Wigan are all in the running.

The Sontli-West TAneashire table is as follows : • Points. P. W. t. D. For Agst:Pts. Runcorn L9igh 8 ... 3 ... 2 ... 3 ... 38— 33 ... 9 Warrington 6 ... 3 ... 2 ... 1 ... 36 35 ... 7 Wigan Widnes 7 ... 3 ... 4 ... 0 ... 21— 22 ... 6 St. Helens

I must again compliment the "A " team on an ex- cellent performance in drawing with Salford at the Willows. There was no scoring but Warrington had rather the best of matters and mide several good efforts to get ahead. The probabilities, prior to the match; were that they would be beaten but the recent successes have made the juniors afraid of no one and they deserved the point they took out of Salford.

• In response to the inquiries of readers of this column I append the results in the Lancashire Com- bination. Warrington stand third in this competition with a record Which must make the first team mem- bers blush. •
The Limeashire Combination table is as follows For Agst.

This Saturday sees .the commencement of the Northern Union Cup Ties, and there will doubtless be a sudden revival of football fever—which however, will very rapidly die away in the camps of the defeated clubs. The first round provides some interesting items,but in the majority of cases, the clubs concerned are of little note. Drawing them in districts has brought many of the better teams together and will save travelling expenses. For .instance Widnes will not have far to go to play Runcorn, and it is very doubtful whether they will go any further. Warring- ton take a short trip to St. Helens, 'where they are promised a warm welcome from the wooden-spoonists Another tough tie is that between T3roaghton Rangers and Oldham, and I fancy the champions will need all the advantage the choice of ground can give them. In Y orkshire the chief engagement is that between Bradford and Huddersfteld,although Sowerby Bridge v. Batley is a match not without interest.

The complete draw for the first round is as follows : Broughton Rngers v. Oldham Outwood Ch v. Todmorden Salford v. Altrincham Ossett v. Otley Leigh v. Swinton Manningham v. Idle St. Helens v. Warrington Castleford v. Thrum Hall Runcorn v. Widnes Wakefield T. v. Holbeck Halifax v. Salterhebble Rochdale H. v. Alverthorpe Bradford v. Huddersfield Dewsbury v. Leeds Hunslet v. Batley South Shields N.. South Goole v. Hull Shields St. Paul's Millom v. Lancaster Wath Brow v. Whitehaven Seaton v. Barrow Recreation Kendal Hrnts v. Morecambe Parton v. Workington Birkenhead v. Werneth Penrith v. ltiatryport.

A meeting of the Northern Union will be held on Monday morning, and the draw made far the second round in time for announcement in the evening papers. The Committee has again decided to draw the clubs in sections, thus :---(l) Lancashire (North of Preston), Cumberland, and Westmoreland; (5) TAncashire (South of Preston) and Cheshire ; (8) Yorkshire and Durham.

I am rather doubtful about the wisdom of pursuing this course, for it appears to narrow the pros- pects of s-Nme c'ubs so much as to leave no room for the , element of luck which is one of the charms of the knock-out competition. There won't be a great many clubs in Section 2 after this Saturday, and if those that are left have to fight it out with one another there will be precious few to uphold the honour of Lancashire in the canclulling stages. The new arrangement seems to give the Yorkshire
clubs a decided advantage, as they are far more numer- ous. However, we shall see how it works out, but r would have preferred an open draw for every round after the first.
Angling.

Some very fine samples of roaell were captured last week end at Mickle Trafford by some of the mem hers of the local Anglers' Association. Mr. James Briars took 28 roach which scaled 15.11b5. The fol- lowing are the weights of some of the largest :-- lib. llozs. 6drs. ; 11b. 7oz. Hrs. ; 11b. 7ozs. sdxs. ; and lib. 4ozs. sdrs. Mr. J. iGreen took one of 6ozs. 6drs..; Mr. W. Hamblett one of lib. 6ozs. ; J. Bowden - one of lib. sozs. Bdrs., and Mr. Thomas • Cooper one of lib. 4ozs. The above are some of the best specimens of roach brought into Warrington for a long time, and are enough to stir up all the latent angling enthusiasm in the district.

SEQUEL TO AN OVERHEAD WIRE PlOlrdas7:, pEL ACCIDENT. Lad' =s. swag &II The Fall from a Tower Wagon. A FRENCH REMEDY bUrEBSEDING BITTER APPLE. PIL COCHIAC, PENNYROYAL, &c. Price Claim for Compensation. 45.6 d. post free. Obtainable:only-from Before His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, a claim under I.VIARTIN, CHEMIST, SOUTHAMPTON the Workmen's Compensation Act was heard in which William Jones, a carter, of 50, Napier-street, claimed £216 9s. from Messrs. R. W. Blackwell and Company, Limited, of City-road, London, engjneers and con- tractors, as compensation for the loss of his son. From the particulars of claim it *appeared that on the 31st October, 1902 the deceased who was a son of the appli- cant, was employed as an assistant wireman by the res- pondents. He was fixing protection wires over the trolley wires of the Warrington Corporation tramways at Scotland-road on the date named when one of the trolley wires btoke and he was knocked from the tower waggon on wllich he was standing, to the ground, a dis- tance of 18f t. He died from the injuries at the In- firmary.—Mr. Cuthbert Smith (instructed by Mr. T. S. Steel) appeared for the applicant and Mr. A. Browne for the respondent company. Mr. Smith explained these circumstances in his open- ing statement, and proceeded to refer to the objecti ons raised in the particulars of claim by the respondents, in which they disputed the particulars, as to the an ture of the alleged accident and cause of death ; as to the earn- ings of the deceased and as to the dependency of the applicant. Mr. Smith said he was prepared to accept Mr. Browne's statement that the average earnings of the deceased were Ll Os. 7d. per week. Mr. Browne said his objections to the claim were four 1! in number, (1) That the deceased was guilty of serious misconduct and negligence ; (2) that the respondents were not undertakers within the meaning of the Act; (3) that the accident did not arise out of his employ- ment; (4) that there was no dependence. Mr. Smith dealt with these points seriatim and then called his witnesses. Ralph Woods, a Carter in the employ of Mr. E. 'lsherwood, who was in charge of the horse drawing the tower waggon, described the accident. The deceased and a man named Edwards, who was the chief linesman, were on the top of the waggon, which was about 18 feet high and was protected on three sides by a rail. The men were fixing guard wires, and as the wires could not be reached from the waggon, the men had a box to stand on. They were not both working on the same side of the wire. After they had been working for about ten minutes witness saw Jones fly over the flap of the waggon into the road. It appeared that a trolley wire struck deceased in the stomach knocking him straight to the ground. He was taken to the Infirmary and died shortly afterwards. By -Mr. Browne: Why couldn't the men both work on the same side of the wire? Witness: They could not work on one side. Further questioned witness said he had never heard anyone warn the deceased not to work on the inside of the wire as it was dangerous. Mr. Browne said there was a terrible curve at the point in question and he was informed that the wire would strike the deceased with a force of fifty tons. ! Joseph Dykes, who was working down below, also gave evidence and said that two men could not work comfortably on one side of the wire. He had never heard of an order that men should not work inside what was termed the strain of the wire. It was dan- gerous to do so, and deceased must have known that it would be dangerous if anything broke. The force would not be fifty tons. Ellen Jones,mother of the deceased, gave evidence as to dependence,and pointed out that owing to ill-health her husband was oftenSunable to work. Respondents offered to pay .£2O in settlement of the action, but this was not accepted. , Mr. Smith then read letters to show, as he put it, how the "magnificent offer" was made. In the first instance suipondonts' solicitors offered:to pay £lO for funeral expenses but denied liability. When this offer was not accepted they again wrote stating that as it would cost them close upon £2O to fight the action, and if they succeeded there was no chance of recovering that amount from the plaintiff,they were instructed to make a final offer—that was to make plaintiff a present of the sum of £2O in full settlement of the claim. William Jones, deceased's father,was also called. For the defence Herbert T. Hawes, resident engineer -for the construction of the wires and trolley standards in Warrington, said that two days previous to the acci- dent he warned the deceased as to the danger of work- ing inside the strain. That was the only occasion on which he warned him. The force with which deceased , would be struck was.about 1,000 pounds. By Mr. Smith: No printed notices of warning as ,to ! the danger of working inside the strain had been issued Edwards would have had the power to order deceased off the car if he did not behave himself properly. George Edwards, foreman linesman, who gave his evi- dence with hesitancy, said he warned the deceased him- self two days previously as to the danger of working , inside the strain. He also warned him five minutes before the accident occurred. Deceased was not stand- ing on the box. Mr. Smith: Was he doing anything wrong ?—Yes. Do you swear that ?—Yes, he was in his wrong place. Did you hear what the Coroner said about you at the inquest ?—Yes. Did he say. you had not created a good impression on his mind ?—Yes. His Honour: Nor have you on mine. Did you say before the Coroner that he was doing nothing wrong ?—No. On being pressed witness still adhered to the state- ment. His Honour: You must understand the question. Did the Coronerask if the deceased man was doing any- thing wrong when he met with the accident ?—Yes. Did you say "no" suppose I-did. Mr. Smith: Do you know the' nature and quality of an oath ?—I have come here to speak the truth. His Honour: You have a very unfortunave way of telling the truth; that is all I can say. Mr. Smith : At the inquest didn't Mr. Steel ask you if you told deceased he was in his wrong place ?—es. Didn't you say "no ? "—I expect I did. His Honour: Yes, of course he did. • Witness still denied that deceased was standing on the box. By Mr. Browne : Witness was seriously ill at the time 2f the inquest, having been so upset by the acci- dent. He did not know what he was doing at the inquest, and did not get over the accident for a few months. His Honour : When you are ill do you generally tell lies ?—No. William James Bailey, secretary to the respondent company, said two men in the employ of the firm had been killed through working inside the strain and the firm recognized the danger of the work. , By Mr. Smith: There were no printed instructions on the waggons which were unprotected on one side. It would be impossible to work if all the sides were pro- tected. After Mr. Browne and Mr. Smith had addressed the court his Honour decided against Mr. Browne on tech- nical points and also held that deceased was not guilty of serious and wilful misconduct. He disbelieved en- tirely the evidence of Edwards and believed that de- ceased did what he did with Edwards' conseat and by, his orders. He awarded applicant the awn of £65 com- pensation.
